text:
📐 250 FACTS ABOUT FREEMASONRY: HISTORY, RITUALS AND FAMOUS MASONS

🏛️ WHAT IS FREEMASONRY?
1. ➡️ Freemasonry is one of the world's oldest and largest fraternal organizations
2. ➡️ It describes itself as "a system of morality, veiled in allegory and illustrated by symbols"
3. ➡️ Its core principles are "Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth"
4. ➡️ French lodges often use "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity" instead
5. ➡️ It teaches moral lessons using the tools and buildings of medieval stonemasons
6. ➡️ The local unit is called a "lodge"
7. ➡️ A group of lodges is governed by a "Grand Lodge"
8. ➡️ An estimated 6 million people worldwide are Freemasons
9. ➡️ The United Grand Lodge of England has around 175,000 members
10. ➡️ In the US, membership peaked at about 4.1 million in 1959
11. ➡️ US membership has since fallen below 1 million
12. ➡️ Freemasonry is not a religion, but members must believe in a Supreme Being
13. ➡️ God is called "the Great Architect of the Universe" in Masonic ritual
14. ➡️ Discussing religion and politics inside the lodge is traditionally forbidden
15. ➡️ Charity is one of Freemasonry's central activities

📜 ORIGINS AND HISTORY
16. ➡️ Freemasonry grew out of the guilds of medieval stonemasons who built cathedrals and castles
17. ➡️ "Freemason" may come from "freestone mason", a skilled carver of fine stone
18. ➡️ The oldest Masonic document is the "Regius Poem", from the early 15th century
19. ➡️ In 1598 and 1599, William Schaw issued the Schaw Statutes for Scottish masons
20. ➡️ The Lodge of Edinburgh (Mary's Chapel) has minutes going back to 1599
21. ➡️ Over time, men who were not builders began to join, called "accepted" or "speculative" Masons
22. ➡️ Antiquarian Elias Ashmole was initiated in 1646, one of the earliest recorded in England
23. ➡️ The first Grand Lodge was founded in London on 24 June 1717
24. ➡️ Four London lodges created it at a dinner at the Goose and Gridiron alehouse
25. ➡️ 24 June is St John the Baptist's Day, an important Masonic feast
26. ➡️ Anthony Sayer was elected the first Grand Master
27. ➡️ James Anderson's "Constitutions of the Free-Masons" came out in 1723
28. ➡️ The Grand Lodge of Scotland was founded in 1736
29. ➡️ In 1751 a rival "Antient" Grand Lodge was formed in England
30. ➡️ The two English grand lodges merged in 1813 to form the United Grand Lodge of England
31. ➡️ Freemasonry spread around the world with the British Empire, trade and armies
32. ➡️ In 1730, Samuel Prichard published "Masonry Dissected", revealing the rituals
33. ➡️ Masonic rituals have been published many times since, so the "secrets" are not truly secret
34. ➡️ The Grand Orient de France was founded in 1773
35. ➡️ In 1877 the Grand Orient de France dropped the requirement to believe in God
36. ➡️ UGLE then withdrew recognition, splitting world Masonry into two main camps
37. ➡️ "Regular" Masonry requires belief in God and a sacred book open in the lodge

🔺 THE THREE DEGREES
38. ➡️ Basic "Craft" or "Blue Lodge" Masonry has three degrees
39. ➡️ The first degree is Entered Apprentice
40. ➡️ The second degree is Fellowcraft
41. ➡️ The third degree is Master Mason
42. ➡️ The degrees are based on the building of King Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem
43. ➡️ The central legend is the story of Hiram Abiff, the Temple's master builder
44. ➡️ In the story, three ruffians demand the secrets of a Master Mason from Hiram
45. ➡️ Hiram refuses to reveal them and is killed
46. ➡️ In American ritual, the three ruffians are named Jubela, Jubelo and Jubelum
47. ➡️ The third-degree ceremony reenacts Hiram's death and symbolic raising
48. ➡️ It teaches fidelity, integrity and the hope of life after death
49. ➡️ A sprig of acacia in the legend symbolizes immortality
50. ➡️ Masonry symbolically names its first three Grand Masters as King Solomon, King Hiram of Tyre and Hiram Abiff

🕯️ RITUALS AND CEREMONIES
51. ➡️ A candidate must ask to join; Masons traditionally do not recruit
52. ➡️ This tradition is summed up as "2B1ASK1": to be one, ask one
53. ➡️ Members vote on each candidate in a secret ballot
54. ➡️ White balls mean yes and black balls mean no
55. ➡️ This is the origin of the word "blackballing"
56. ➡️ During initiation the candidate wears a blindfold called a "hoodwink"
57. ➡️ The blindfold symbolizes darkness before receiving "light"
58. ➡️ A rope called a "cable tow" is placed around him
59. ➡️ He traditionally has one trouser leg rolled up, one shoe slipped off and his left breast bared
60. ➡️ He kneels at the altar to take an "obligation", a solemn promise
61. ➡️ He swears on the holy book of his own faith
62. ➡️ That book can be the Bible, the Quran, the Torah, the Vedas or another scripture
63. ➡️ The obligation includes promises to help others, act honestly and keep Masonic secrets
64. ➡️ Old obligations included gruesome symbolic penalties
65. ➡️ England removed those penalties from its ritual in 1986
66. ➡️ The candidate is then "brought to light" as the blindfold is removed
67. ➡️ He is presented with a white lambskin apron
68. ➡️ The apron is the badge of a Mason, symbolizing innocence and purity
69. ➡️ He is taught secret signs, handshakes called "grips", and passwords
70. ➡️ These "modes of recognition" let Masons identify each other
71. ➡️ After each degree, the new member hears a lecture explaining its symbols
72. ➡️ Some lodges use painted "tracing boards" to illustrate these lessons
73. ➡️ A Masonic funeral includes placing a sprig of acacia on the coffin
74. ➡️ New lodge buildings may have their cornerstone laid in a Masonic ceremony
75. ➡️ The cornerstone is traditionally laid in the northeast corner of a building

🏠 INSIDE A LODGE
76. ➡️ The lodge room is a symbolic copy of King Solomon's Temple
77. ➡️ The leader, the Worshipful Master, sits in the East, where the sun rises
78. ➡️ The Senior Warden sits in the West and the Junior Warden in the South
79. ➡️ The floor often has a black-and-white checkered pavement
80. ➡️ The checkered floor symbolizes the good and bad, light and dark of human life
81. ➡️ Two pillars represent the bronze pillars of Solomon's Temple, Boaz and Jachin
82. ➡️ An altar stands in the centre with the sacred book, square and compasses
83. ➡️ The Tyler guards the door with a sword to keep out non-members
84. ➡️ The word "Tyler" may come from the tilers who protected a building's roof
85. ➡️ A non-Mason who tries to learn the secrets is called a "cowan"
86. ➡️ In many American lodges the Worshipful Master wears a hat during meetings
87. ➡️ Masonic years are counted "Anno Lucis", "in the year of light", adding 4,000 years
88. ➡️ The son of a Mason is traditionally called a "Lewis"

🔣 SYMBOLS
89. ➡️ The square and compasses is the best-known Masonic emblem
90. ➡️ The square stands for morality and fair dealing
91. ➡️ The compasses stand for keeping one's desires within proper bounds
92. ➡️ In many countries a letter "G" sits in the middle
93. ➡️ The "G" is said to stand for God and for Geometry
94. ➡️ The rough ashlar, an unworked stone, represents a man before Masonic teaching
95. ➡️ The perfect ashlar, a smooth finished stone, represents an improved man
96. ➡️ The Entered Apprentice's tools are the 24-inch gauge and the common gavel
97. ➡️ The 24-inch gauge teaches dividing the 24 hours of a day wisely
98. ➡️ The Fellowcraft's tools are the square, the level and the plumb
99. ➡️ The Master Mason's tool is the trowel, to spread "brotherly love"
100. ➡️ The "All-Seeing Eye" became a Masonic symbol in the 1790s
101. ➡️ It appeared in Masonic use after it was adopted on the US Great Seal in 1782
102. ➡️ The beehive symbolizes hard work and cooperation
103. ➡️ The anchor and ark symbolize hope and a well-grounded faith

🗣️ WORDS AND PHRASES
104. ➡️ "On the level" comes from the Mason's level, meaning honest and fair
105. ➡️ "On the square" means acting honestly with others
106. ➡️ "Getting the third degree" is often linked to the intense third-degree ceremony
107. ➡️ Masons "meet on the level and part on the square"
108. ➡️ "So mote it be", meaning "so may it be", ends Masonic prayers

➕ HIGHER DEGREES AND RELATED GROUPS
109. ➡️ Master Mason is the highest degree of basic Masonry
110. ➡️ Optional further degrees are offered by "appendant bodies"
111. ➡️ The Scottish Rite offers degrees numbered up to 33
112. ➡️ Despite its name, the Scottish Rite developed mostly in France and the US
113. ➡️ The 33rd degree is honorary and awarded for outstanding service
114. ➡️ The York Rite includes the Royal Arch, Cryptic Masonry and the Knights Templar
115. ➡️ Masonic Knights Templar orders are open only to Christian Masons
116. ➡️ The Shriners were founded in New York in 1870 by Walter Fleming and William Florence
117. ➡️ Shriners are famous for their red fez hats
118. ➡️ The Shriners opened their first children's hospital in Shreveport, Louisiana, in 1922
119. ➡️ Shriners Hospitals for Children treat children regardless of their family's ability to pay
120. ➡️ The Order of DeMolay for young men was founded in 1919 in Kansas City
121. ➡️ The Order of the Rainbow for Girls was founded in 1922
122. ➡️ Job's Daughters International was founded in 1920
123. ➡️ The Order of the Eastern Star admits Master Masons and their female relatives

♀️ WOMEN AND FREEMASONRY
124. ➡️ Regular Freemasonry admits only men
125. ➡️ Elizabeth Aldworth of Ireland is said to have secretly witnessed a lodge meeting in the early 1700s
126. ➡️ She was reportedly initiated to keep the secret, becoming the "Lady Freemason"
127. ➡️ In France, "Lodges of Adoption" for women appeared in the 18th century
128. ➡️ Maria Deraismes was initiated into a French lodge in 1882
129. ➡️ In 1893 she co-founded "Le Droit Humain", which admits men and women equally
130. ➡️ The Order of Women Freemasons was founded in England in 1908
131. ➡️ In 1999 UGLE said England's two women's grand lodges were regular in practice, though separate

🌍 PRINCE HALL FREEMASONRY
132. ➡️ In 1775 Prince Hall and 14 other Black men were initiated in Boston
133. ➡️ They were initiated by a lodge attached to a British army regiment
134. ➡️ In 1784 they received a warrant from England for African Lodge No. 459
135. ➡️ This became the root of Prince Hall Freemasonry
136. ➡️ Today most US grand lodges and UGLE recognize Prince Hall grand lodges
137. ➡️ Famous Prince Hall Masons include Thurgood Marshall, Duke Ellington and Shaquille O'Neal

🇺🇸 FREEMASONRY AND AMERICA
138. ➡️ George Washington became a Mason in Fredericksburg, Virginia, in 1752
139. ➡️ He was sworn in as president in 1789 on a Bible from St. John's Lodge No. 1 in New York
140. ➡️ In 1793 Washington laid the cornerstone of the US Capitol in a Masonic ceremony
141. ➡️ Benjamin Franklin became Grand Master of Pennsylvania in 1734
142. ➡️ That year he printed Anderson's Constitutions, the first Masonic book printed in America
143. ➡️ Paul Revere served as Grand Master of Massachusetts
144. ➡️ About 9 of the 56 signers of the Declaration of Independence are believed to have been Masons
145. ➡️ Fourteen US presidents were Masons
146. ➡️ Harry Truman served as Grand Master of Missouri from 1940 to 1941
147. ➡️ Gerald Ford was the last US president known to be a Mason
148. ➡️ Lyndon B. Johnson received only the first degree
149. ➡️ The Grand Lodge of New York laid the cornerstone of the Statue of Liberty's pedestal in 1884
150. ➡️ The Statue of Liberty's sculptor, Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, was a Mason
151. ➡️ The George Washington Masonic National Memorial in Virginia was dedicated in 1932
152. ➡️ The Scottish Rite's "House of the Temple" in Washington, DC, was completed in 1915
153. ➡️ Explorers Meriwether Lewis and William Clark were both Masons
154. ➡️ Mohawk leader Joseph Brant was initiated in London in 1776

⚠️ OPPOSITION AND PERSECUTION
155. ➡️ In 1738 Pope Clement XII banned Catholics from joining Freemasonry
156. ➡️ The ban was reaffirmed in 1983 and again in 2023
157. ➡️ The Church says Catholics who join are in "grave sin"
158. ➡️ In 1826 New Yorker William Morgan vanished after threatening to publish Masonic rituals
159. ➡️ His disappearance sparked a huge anti-Masonic movement in the US
160. ➡️ The Anti-Masonic Party, formed in 1828, was America's first major third party
161. ➡️ In 1831 it held the first national presidential nominating convention in US history
162. ➡️ Mussolini's Italy banned Freemasonry in 1925
163. ➡️ Nazi Germany dissolved lodges and persecuted Freemasons
164. ➡️ Franco's Spain also banned Freemasonry and persecuted its members
165. ➡️ Many conspiracy theories about Masons are rooted in antisemitism

One Texas lawmaker is already looking to limit Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's power. News Nation's Xavier Walton reports, State Rep Brian Harrison posted on social media that she was set to, "inherit the powers of a DICTATOR"...: “He said in part, you know, we still have total power in Texas. But Harrison wants Governor Abbott to pass a similar bill that he filed back in 22, essentially calling it a threat to our constitutional system, a divided government, some of the things that he wants to limit prohibiting the governor from suspending or modifying statutes or from reissuing expired or rejecting emergency orders, and also emergency orders that are subject to judicial review. ”
Harrison says it's not about a Democrat governor, and that he introduced the same bill after Republican Gregg Abbott was elected.

Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan is calling for a new majority leader when Democrats take over the Senate in January.: “When it comes to exactly who that is, I can't tell you that, um, but, uh, I think that people are ready for new voices and new leadership in the Senate caucus. ”
76-year-old Chuck Schumer has led the caucus since 2017, and says he expects to remain the leader.

First Lady Melania Trump brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at the White House, hoping a temporary ceasefire can help pave the way toward ending the war.: “The first lady discussed the six day pause in fighting she helped arrange in the Russian occupied city of Oleki. I became aware of the severity of the humanitarian crisis in Olechki in September. Recognizing the urgency, I acted immediately. The temporary ceasefire allowed humanitarian aid to reach residents in. Nearly 800 people to be evacuated. I was involved in every stage of the planning, she says. She hopes a humanitarian effort can build trust and open the door to a broader peace agreement. Together we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire, Stacy Linn Worldwide News Network, Washington. ”

Airlines affected included Wizz Air, Finnair, Ryanair, one of the biggest airlines in Europe, Aer Lingus, and more. ”
None of those threats were found to be credible.

The burger chain also adopted a “poison pill” plan to prevent a hostile takeover.

The annual Christmas village is up in Bryant Park, and the Rockettes have kicked off their Christmas Spectacular at Radio City Music Hall.

text:
One Decision | The Peace Offer That Came With a Date for War

85 years ago today, Nov 5, 1941, Tokyo: Japan's leaders approved two final offers of peace to the United States. The same document set a date for war.

In Washington, US Navy code-breakers read the deadline that same day. What they could not read was what it was for.

The meeting was an Imperial Conference, held in the presence of Emperor Hirohito. Prime Minister Hideki Tojo, the chiefs of the army and navy general staffs and senior ministers ratified a paper called "Essentials for Carrying Out the Empire's Policies."

It did two things at once.

Talks with Washington would go on, with two proposals. Plan A offered to withdraw troops from China and French Indochina once peace with China was signed, but kept forces in parts of China for an unstated "suitable period." Plan B, the fallback, was a short-term deal: Japan would leave southern Indochina, and the US would resume trade and supply oil.

In the same paper, Japan resolved on war with the United States, Britain and the Netherlands. Force would be used in early December. Only success in the talks would stop it.

Why the hurry? Oil. Since the summer, when the US, Britain and the Dutch froze Japanese assets, Japan's reserves had been running down. At the conference, Tojo put it bluntly: "Two years from now we will have no petroleum for military use. Ships will stop moving." He feared Japan "would become a third-class nation after 2 or 3 years if we just sat tight."

The navy moved the same day. Navy Order No. 1 told Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto to complete preparations for war "within the first ten days of December." Aboard his flagship Nagato in Saeki Bay, Yamamoto issued Combined Fleet Top Secret Operation Order No. 1, the master plan for war against the US, Britain and the Netherlands.

Its section on Hawaii was left blank in the general order. Only the carrier and submarine forces were given the details, and the plan was kept secret even from the rest of the fleet. Two days later, Order No. 2 named a tentative opening day: December 8, Tokyo time.

Foreign Minister Shigenori Togo also cabled his ambassador in Washington, Kichisaburo Nomura: "it is absolutely necessary that all arrangements for the signing of this agreement be completed by the 25th of this month."

He gave no reason. The US Navy decrypted and translated the cable on Nov 5. Washington now knew there was a deadline. It did not know a fleet was being readied behind it.

So when was the deadline? Sources differ, because there were two clocks.

The conference document set the cutoff at 00:00 on December 1, Tokyo time, in effect the end of November 30. Nobutaka Ike's translation of the conference records reads "midnight of December 1."

The diplomats were given an earlier date, November 25. On November 22, Togo moved it to the 29th: "let me write it out for you-twenty-ninth." Then he added: "After that things are automatically going to happen." Some histories, including the US Army's, give these November dates as the deadline. Both are right. They were deadlines for different people.

What followed ran close to the timetable. Plan A reached Secretary of State Cordell Hull on Nov 7, Plan B on Nov 20. On Nov 26 (Tokyo date), the carrier force sailed from the Kuril Islands, under orders to turn back if the talks succeeded. On Nov 26 in Washington, Hull handed over the American reply. It offered nothing Tokyo would accept.

On December 1, a second Imperial Conference decided on war.

The meeting of Nov 5 did not quite choose war. It chose a clock. From then on, peace needed a breakthrough. War needed only for nothing to happen.

text:
#H5N1 
[Maeve Cullinan brings us an excellent summary of the current state of play.]

➡️ ⚠️Is America on the brink of sparking a new flu pandemic?

- Virologists fear ⚠️ the United States is inching closer to becoming ground zero for an H5N1 contagion

- America is closer than ever to harbouring the next flu pandemic, leading experts have warned.

- H5N1, the avian flu that has decimated bird populations worldwide, is ➡️ spreading through US cattle herds, raging on one of the country’s largest mink farms and, in the past few weeks, has infected three people in Washington state, one of whom has died.

- The new cases bring the total number of people in the US infected with H5N1 since 2022 to 75. There have been three deaths.

- Scientists say ➡️ deep cuts to the federal agencies responsible for protecting human and animal health under the Trump administration have allowed the virus to spread largely unchecked, sharply raising the risk of a human outbreak.

- ⚠️The more the virus circulates in animals, the more people are exposed to it, and the more chances it has to adapt to humans, experts say.

- H5N1 has shown no sign so far of spreading between people, but if it did, it is feared the virus could trigger a global pandemic with a very high human cost.

- The Telegraph spoke to leading virologists, many of whom argue that America is getting closer to becoming ground zero for the next flu pandemic.

- It would not be the first time. ➡️ The first case of H1N1, the “Spanish flu”, is thought to have emerged at an army base in Kansas in March 1918, and the pandemic went on to kill more than 50 million people.

- ➡️ “It does feel like a disaster waiting to happen,” said Prof Ed Hutchinson, a molecular and cellular virologist at the University of Glasgow.

- “We keep having a series of near misses, and I wonder how long our luck is going to hold.”

- A preventable outbreak

- ➡️ H5N1 reached the US in 2021, carried by wild birds that had migrated from Europe.

- For two years, it behaved much as it has elsewhere.
It infected farmed poultry, forcing mass culls at chicken and turkey farms, and occasionally jumped to mammals that had fed on infected carcasses, including seals, dolphins, bears, coyotes and foxes.

- The same scenario has played out across the world, including in Britain, where more than three million farmed birds have been culled since 2020 in an attempt to stamp out the virus.

- But ➡️ in late 2023, there was a significant and unusual development in the US.

- ➡️ At a cattle farm in Texas, ➡️ H5N1 infected a single dairy cow, most likely through contact with infected bird droppings in its feed. In most mammals, the virus quickly dies out, but this time it began spreading rapidly from cow to cow.

- ➡️ Within months, hundreds of herds across more than 12 states had been infected.

- ➡️ In the US, cows are often raised on farms in one state and then moved to large commercial milking centres in another, meaning that ➡️ at any given time thousands of animals are being moved across the country.

- Because cows infected with H5N1 do not always show obvious signs of illness, hundreds of ➡️ thousands of sick cattle have been unwittingly moved across state lines, bringing the virus into new regions.

- The practice has been heavily criticised for the biosecurity risk it carries.

- ➡️ “The cow infections have been totally preventable,” said Marc Johnson, a virologist at the University of Missouri.

- “Cattle infection usually lasts a few weeks, and then they recover. ➡️ If they just separated the infected herds or animals until it fizzled, then it would stop. ➡️But they keep moving cattle around and spreading it to new states.”

- 🚨 Surveillance efforts on cattle farms have also been significantly wound down under the Trump administration.

- “There was a lot of openness and transparency at the end of the Biden administration, and they were really open about some of the challenges in getting farms to open up to testing,” Dr Devi Sridhar, a professor of global health at the University of Edinburgh, told The Telegraph.

- 🚨 “Then Trump came in, and everything went quiet. And I don’t think it went quiet because it went away. It went quiet because they just stopped tracking it.”

- Of the 75 human cases in the US, at least 50 have been linked directly to cattle farming, meaning the outbreak in cows has become the main route by which the virus is reaching people.

- ➡️ Most human cases linked to cattle have been mild, and far less dangerous than historic cases linked to infections from wild or farmed birds. ➡️ Of the roughly 1,000 human cases of H5N1 linked to birds since it first emerged in China in 1997, around half have died.

- But ➡️ on November 1, the first person to be infected with the cow variant of H5N1, known as ➡️ genotype B.13, was confirmed to have died.

- The individual, who worked on a farm in Washington where at least 40 herds have been infected with H5N1, had underlying health conditions, which may have exacerbated the disease, and ➡️ died shortly after becoming sick – but the development is still of concern, say experts.

- ➡️ “This goes against the pattern of mild disease when infected from dairy cattle, versus severe disease when infected from birds, which is worrying given the circulation in cattle,” said Dr Sridhar.

- Reassortment risks

- One of the ➡️ biggest fears among scientists is that bird flu could combine with ordinary seasonal influenza to create a new strain capable of spreading easily between people.

- ➡️ “This is a time of year when we can expect to see more ➡️ circulation of [human] seasonal influenza,” said Dr Marion Koopmans, professor of public health virology at Erasmus MC Medical Centre in the Netherlands.

- 🚨 “A bad scenario would be that someone working with cattle brought the ‘regular’ human flu in, got [H5N1] on top of that, and that ➡️ develops into a mix that can spread but to which people have less immunity.

- “The chances of such an event are very low, but it is a concern shared among virologists.”

- ➡️ The process, known as reassortment, occurs when two flu viruses infect the same animal or person and exchange genetic material, potentially creating a new strain.

- ➡️ Scientists are particularly concerned as H5N1 spreads beyond cattle and into other mammals – chiefly mink.

- ➡️ For more than two months, an outbreak has raged on ➡️ an Utah farm housing thousands of mink, according to an investigation by US news outlet ProPublica.

- Mink farms have previously been described as 
🚨potential pandemic “time bombs”, because their respiratory systems are similar to those of humans, meaning viruses spread easily between them and people.

- ➡️ Despite calls for the animals to be culled, ➡️ Utah officials have so far refused to mandate action, ProPublica reported.

- The investigation also suggested that ➡️ state officials were prioritising the financial interests of the fur industry, which exports much of its produce to China and Russia, while federal authorities had failed to intervene.

- ➡️ H5N1 has previously spread through mink farms in Spain and Finland, but authorities in those countries took much tougher action.

- “There was really vigorous state intervention and culling. In Finland, they used widespread culling and vaccination programmes,” said Prof Hutchinson.

- “It doesn’t sound like there’s been a great deal of enthusiasm for intervention [in the US] on behalf of the authorities.

- “So you have this ongoing situation where the virus is replicating on a mink farm, which would be an ideal situation for the virus to slowly adapt to something more suitable to humans.

- “As we move into the flu season, more and more of the people are also likely to be carrying human influenza at the same time [as potentially being infected with H5N1].”

- Prof Hutchinson also warned that ➡️ the vulnerability of some farm workers could make the outbreak harder to monitor.

- ➡️ “In the US system, a lot of the people working in the farming sector are undocumented workers. ➡️ They are less likely to be engaged with public health surveillance than some other groups for obvious reasons,” he said.

- ➡️ Reassortment has been the cause of several major flu pandemics.

- ➡️ In 2009, a new strain of H1N1, commonly known as swine flu, emerged in Mexico and spread around the world within months, ultimately causing an estimated 150,000 deaths.

- ➡️ The virus emerged after ➡️ different strains of bird, pig and human influenza exchanged genetic material, creating a new strain to which much of the population had little existing immunity.

- Several countries, including Britain, have stockpiled supplies of H5N1 vaccines designed for humans, in preparation for the possibility that the virus begins spreading between people.

- The US holds a federal stockpile of five million doses of bird flu vaccine. The doses are grown and cultured inside chicken eggs, the traditional method of manufacturing seasonal flu jabs.

- While effective, the process is relatively slow, and experts have warned that producing enough vaccines to meet demand in a pandemic could take months.

- ➡️ In May last year, 🚨 US health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a vaccine sceptic, cancelled a $766 million contract with Moderna to develop an mRNA vaccine against H5N1 – a technology that could offer a much faster way of delivering vaccines than traditional egg-based production. He said the technology “poses more risks than benefits” for respiratory viruses - a view that experts said was baseless.

- ➡️ “This is how outbreaks happen,” Dr Krutika Kuppalli, associate professor in the Division of Infectious Diseases at the University of Texas Southwestern said.

- ➡️ “You have continued spread of the disease; you’re not controlling it, and ➡️ it allows the virus to evolve. So at some point, we’ll potentially see more human cases.

- “If we develop human-to-human spread, that could really set things off.”

- ➡️ The “blue tsunami” brought in by the US midterms could offer some hope, experts say.

- Many hope that a new wave of Democrats in the House and Senate will ➡️ put pressure on Trump to protect science funding and reinstate some of the people and departments fired in deep federal cuts to the US Centers for Disease Control and US Department of Agriculture last year.

- “We’re hoping you’ll have more [strong] voices going into government, and more scientific transparency,” said Dr Sridhar.

By Maeve Cullinan

text:
Washington went looking for cheaper diesel and potash. It picked a trade fight with Canada, then tried to source both from Moscow’s orbit. It is back at the Canadian negotiating table with a weaker hand. That sequence tells you more about this administration’s dealmaking than any White House announcement.

The commercial results so far are worth laying out plainly:

• Diesel: The Financial Times reports that two of three tankers sent from Russia toward the US changed course after failing to find American buyers.

• Buyers: Warnings from Congress and state authorities made the political risk too expensive for US companies to take on.

• Potash: Belarusian shipments remain limited and have to move through St Petersburg. Baltic states have refused to reopen their ports or ease sanctions despite US pressure.

A tanker changing course matters. The companies asked to receive the diesel were looking beyond the immediate price of a cargo. They had to consider the legal and political exposure of building a business around a sanctions carve-out that Congress or a future administration could challenge. On that calculation, the cargo was a lousy deal.

But the US market was never the whole sanctions question. Even negligible American purchases can give Moscow a useful precedent if relaxed restrictions make Russian diesel easier to sell to third countries. A shipment rejected in the US can still earn the Kremlin money somewhere else. The next step cannot be a victory lap over two diverted tankers. Congress needs to make its position clear, and companies in other markets need a credible warning about the consequences of handling these sales. Any sanctions relief also needs to be reversed through the available legal channels. Commercial caution has limited the damage in America; it cannot substitute for policy.

The potash route exposes a different constraint. Belarus may have product to sell, and Washington may want it, but the Baltic states control the ports that would make the obvious route work. They refused to bend. Sending limited volumes through St Petersburg adds a long, awkward detour to a scheme supposedly designed to improve supply and prices. Those governments understood that access to their ports is a decision they get to make, whatever deal the White House hoped to announce.

Canada was right there.

Canada is the leading exporter of potash to the US. It also produces large volumes of fuel from its own resources, with a shorter route to northern American states than diesel shipped north from the southern US. Production costs for diesel in Canada and the US are broadly comparable; transport distance can matter to the delivered price. A workable trade agreement with Ottawa offered Washington a far more direct way to address both products.

Instead, Trump’s tariff war turned a close supplier into a negotiating adversary. The two sides had reportedly worked toward a new agreement that could have ended the dispute. Days before signing, the White House added demands Canada would not accept. Washington then spent months treating Ottawa’s refusal to surrender its own interests as some great offense. The administration searched for Belarusian potash and Russian diesel while the Canadian option remained tangled in tariffs the Canadians had imposed themselves.

A real price mechanism operates here, though nobody should pretend one agreement could set fuel prices by decree. Removing reciprocal trade barriers, including US tariffs affecting Canadian potash and diesel, could ease costs along existing supply routes. Whether that reaches consumers depends on volumes, transport and the wider market. At least that approach starts with a supplier already deeply integrated into the US economy. Chasing cargoes through sanctioned Russian and Belarusian routes starts with political risk, uncertain buyers and blocked ports.

After the election loss, Washington’s posture toward Canada changed. Prime Minister Mark Carney described the American position this way: “They are now asking for less and offering more, but we have not reached an agreement.” Ottawa is in no rush.

Of course it isn’t. The US walked away from an earlier path to a deal, tried to pressure Canada, and then discovered that the alternative purchases were much harder to execute than the sales pitch implied. Carney can now see Washington’s need more clearly than Washington can hide it. Canada may not get every term it wants. It does mean the White House has spent its own influence for very little return.

The hard policy lesson is bigger than Trump’s embarrassment. Sanctions, ports and trade relationships are connected. You cannot loosen a restriction for a quick domestic headline and assume the benefit stays confined to the US market. You cannot pressure allied governments into opening infrastructure they have chosen to keep closed. And you cannot wage a tariff war against your nearest practical supplier, then expect that supplier to sign on your old timetable when your backup plan fails.

American firms and Baltic governments held their ground. Washington should now close the diesel loophole before third-country sales turn a failed US import deal into a revenue opportunity for Moscow. Then it can negotiate with Canada on terms that actually serve American buyers. Ottawa has every reason to read the fine print this time.

text:
U.S. Treasury Signals Possible Shift in Debt Financing Strategy for 2027
In Washington today, the United States Treasury has kept its near-term bond auctions steady, yet a quiet change in official language has opened the door to a different way of financing America’s growing debt as early as 2027.
In its November 4 quarterly refunding statement, the Treasury said it anticipates maintaining current auction sizes for nominal coupon securities and floating-rate notes for the next several quarters. 
It removed the earlier phrase “at least.” 
Analysts view that small edit as preserving flexibility for later adjustments.
A possible path in 2027 would involve modestly reducing sales of the longest bonds, especially 20-year and 30-year issues, while increasing shorter- and intermediate-term borrowing. 
The total amount of debt would not shrink. 
Only the maturity mix would change. 
The government would still refinance large sums and fund ongoing needs, but a greater share would be rolled over more frequently.
This approach can benefit the United States by helping manage long-term interest costs. 
Long bonds lock in rates for decades. 
When demand softens or uncertainty rises, yields climb and the interest bill grows. Reducing the supply of those longest securities can ease upward pressure on long-term yields, supporting the Treasury’s goal of borrowing at the lowest sustainable cost over time. 
The trade-off is more frequent refinancing of the shorter debt.
The scale remains substantial. Treasury projects roughly 618 billion dollars in privately held net marketable borrowing for the October-to-December 2026 quarter and about 800 billion dollars for January-to-March 2027. It plans to offer 125 billion dollars to refinance approximately 97 billion dollars of maturing notes and bonds, raising roughly 28 billion dollars in new cash.
For the U.S. dollar, the effects would flow mainly through yields and confidence. 
Easing pressure on long-term yields can reduce one traditional support for the currency by making longer-duration U.S. assets relatively less attractive to foreign capital. 
Heavier short-term issuance also raises rollover frequency; later rate moves or fiscal concerns could introduce periods of softness. 
Credible cost management tends to support the dollar; any perception of weaker structural demand for Treasuries can weigh on it.
Gold prices typically respond to real yields, the dollar, and the fiscal backdrop. 
Successful moderation of long-term yields lowers the opportunity cost of holding gold and can be supportive. 
A softer dollar, should it emerge, would also tend to lift gold. Persistent large financing needs reinforce the longer-term fiscal narrative many investors already associate with the metal.
Silver generally moves with gold but carries a strong industrial component in solar, electronics, electric vehicles, and manufacturing. 
Any yield or dollar support that lifts gold often transmits to silver, frequently with higher volatility. Lower long-term rates can also ease financing conditions for the industrial sectors that consume silver. 
At the same time, silver’s industrial exposure means it can diverge if growth or investment slows. 
In a scenario of contained borrowing costs and steady confidence, both metals can benefit, with silver potentially amplifying the move.
The bottom line is clear. 
This is an indication that officials are keeping future financing options open as borrowing needs evolve. 
Managing the structure and cost of debt is becoming as important as simply financing it. 
The announcement does not cancel any debt, announce a global reset, or signal a currency revaluation. It simply shows continued evaluation of how best to manage America’s substantial obligations.
Sources include the Reuters report on the Treasury language shift and the official Quarterly Refunding Statement from Assistant Secretary for Financial Markets Hunter McMaster.

text:
𝗕𝘂𝗿𝗴𝘂𝗺’𝘀 𝗕𝗹𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿
There is a coherent, if speculative, argument that DOI Sec. Burgum’s Order 3454 could have cost Republicans votes in a subset of close races—particularly in Western or public-lands-adjacent districts—through the mechanism of motivated, single-issue or multi-issue voters who already viewed federal public-lands policy as tilted too far toward commercial extraction.
Opinion By: Capt. William E. Simpson II - USMM Ret. - Rancher-Wild Horse Researcher
The case rests on existing opinion data, the size and intensity of certain constituencies, the narrow margins in several contests, and the order’s explicit prioritization of livestock over other uses. It does not rest on any direct polling that tested the order itself due to a short window between Burgum’s announcement of the Order (Oct. 28th) and Nov. 3rd, 2026.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗹𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗲𝗻𝘃𝗶𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
Polling on public lands consistently shows broad, often bipartisan concern about management that prioritizes commercial or extractive uses over wildlife, recreation, and long-term ecological condition. Center for Western Priorities and Colorado College State of the Rockies surveys in recent cycles have found majorities (frequently 70–85%+) in Mountain West states viewing rollbacks of wildlife and land protections as a serious problem, and large majorities preferring to keep public lands in public hands rather than expand commercial access at the expense of other values. Opposition to treating public lands primarily as a revenue stream for a narrow set of interests is not fringe; it appears across party lines when the question is framed around wildlife, open space, or local recreation access.Wild-horse constituencies amplify this. Advocacy organizations, online communities, and adoption/rescue networks have built a durable, emotionally engaged audience that treats roundups, fertility control, and forage allocation as core issues. While the absolute number of pure single-issue wild-horse voters is smaller than the broader public-lands or wildlife electorate, these voters are high-intensity: they track BLM and Interior actions closely, share information rapidly, and have demonstrated willingness to contact officials and mobilize around specific policy moves.
Order 3454’s language directing accelerated reductions of wild horses and burros “to the maximum extent practicable,” tracking of fertility-control treatments ($30-million to be spent on using an EPA registered pesticide, PZP, to sterilize wild horses) and progress toward AML to free forage for livestock maps directly onto the priorities this group has long opposed.
𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝘃𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀
The theoretical pathway is straightforward:• Order 3454 was framed by its supporters as helping ranchers, cutting red tape, and using managed grazing for wildfire reduction. Critics (including wild-horse and some wildlife groups) described it as a systematic elevation of livestock AUMs above wildlife, native predators, and free-roaming equines, with concrete directives to expand grazing, reinstate suspended AUMs, and accelerate horse reductions.
For voters already inclined to see public-lands policy as captured by commercial interests, the order supplied a fresh, high-profile confirmation issued by a Cabinet secretary one week before Election Day.
• In close races, the relevant voters need not be large in absolute numbers. Margins measured in dozens to a few thousand votes (as reported in several Senate and House contests) mean that even a modest number of motivated defectors, lower-intensity Republicans who stayed home, or independent/crossover voters who shifted can decide the outcome. A subset of these voters may treat public-lands and wildlife issues as secondary but still salient enough to tip a decision when other factors are close.
• The one-week window limited mass-media penetration, but it is long enough for targeted dissemination. Advocacy networks, Substack writers, social-media accounts focused on public lands or wild horses, and local conservation groups can move information to their existing audiences faster than general news cycles. Voters who already follow these channels would have seen the order framed as an attack on wildlife and wild horses rather than as a rancher-support measure.
𝗦𝗰𝗼𝗽𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗴𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
This mechanism is most plausible in districts or states with meaningful public-lands acreage, outdoor-recreation economies, or visible wild-horse populations (parts of the Mountain West, certain rural or exurban districts elsewhere). It is less plausible as a decisive factor in urban or Eastern races where public lands are abstract. It also competes with larger, longer-running drivers—cost of living, the Middle East conflict and energy prices, overall presidential approval—that dominated most post-election analysis.
The order’s own framing around wildfire mitigation and domestic meat production could have neutralized or even attracted some ranching-community or rural voters who prioritize those https://t.co/WycajsAD5v short, the argument is that Order 3454 supplied a concrete, late-cycle signal of commercial prioritization on public lands to constituencies that already held strong views on the issue and that, in races decided by very small absolute numbers of votes, even a limited mobilization or defection effect among those constituencies could have been enough to flip the result.
Whether that actually occurred in any specific race remains unmeasured; the absence of direct polling does not disprove the possibility, but it also means the claim stays in the realm of plausible mechanism rather than demonstrated causation.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹: 𝗮 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗪𝗛𝗙𝗕 𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗱𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
The same opinion environment and the same narrow margins create a symmetrical argument for the opposite outcome. Had Brenda Younkin (Deputy Assistant Secretary for Lands and Minerals Management), after receiving and reviewing the materials forwarded through Will Boothby in the May 13, 2026 email chain, briefed Secretary Burgum on the Wild Horse Fire Brigade (WHFB) plan and secured a public, affirmative administration statement or pilot commitment before Election Day, the same high-intensity public-lands, wildlife, and wild-horse constituencies could have been moved in the Republican direction.
The plan, as outlined in the March 11, 2026 correspondence and subsequent materials, proposes relocating excess horses (via existing authorities such as the Humane Transfer of Excess Animals Act and BLM IM-2022-035) into remote wilderness areas unsuited for commercial livestock, where natural predation maintains population stability; reducing fine fuels that drive catastrophic wildfire and toxic smoke; freeing forage on conflict allotments for ranchers; and addressing the public-health burden of wildfire smoke.
It is framed as legal under current statute, beneficial to livestock producers under FLPMA multiple-use principles, protective of wild-horse genetics and cultural heritage, and aligned with both wildfire mitigation and taxpayer savings.Independent reporting and data support core elements of that framing.
AM Best’s March 2026 podcast interviewed William Simpson specifically on novel toxins from super-hot wildfires, the public-health and insurance risks, and the cost of holding horses versus deploying them for fuel reduction, citing the roughly $150 million annual off-range holding figure.
NPR covered the same proposal to use BLM-held horses for wildfire mitigation rather than long-term captivity.
Epoch Times, Reasons to be Cheerful, Arizona Highways, OPB, and other outlets have reported on Simpson’s multi-year immersion observations (including the 2018 Klamathon Fire) and the plan’s logic.
On the underlying numbers: Congressional Research Service, E&E News/POLITICO, and BLM’s own data confirm that off-range holding routinely consumes $100–109 million per year—roughly two-thirds of the program’s $142–153 million budget—for tens of thousands of animals. UCLA’s 2024 Science Advances study (Connolly et al.) estimated 52,480–55,710 premature deaths in California alone from wildfire-smoke PM2.5 between 2008 and 2018, with an associated economic impact of $432–456 billion; broader U.S. analyses have placed annual attributable deaths in the low-to-mid tens of thousands.
The Klamathon Fire (July 5–21, 2018) burned 38,008 acres in Siskiyou County, California, according to contemporaneous incident reports and Wikipedia. Simpson served nine days as an unpaid local-knowledge technical advisor to CAL FIRE commanders. Multiple independent outlets (NPR, OPB, Arizona Highways) reported his first-hand observations that areas previously grazed by the local herd (estimated at roughly 5,000 acres of moderated fuels in some accounts) limited fire intensity, provided safer staging zones for personnel and equipment, and helped prevent advance into the Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument. These accounts describe horses remaining calm and continuing to graze near the fire front rather than panicking.
USFS budget trends further contextualize the cost argument.
Multiple analyses (including Forest Service reports cited by Wildfire Today and Taxpayer Network fact sheets) document that fire suppression and preparedness have grown to dominate the agency’s discretionary appropriations—rising from roughly 16% in 1995 to more than 50% in recent years when wildfire adjustment funds are included—while hazardous-fuels reduction, forest management, and prevention remain substantially smaller line items.
Salaries and expenses constitute a large share across accounts.
This allocation structure leaves limited resources for proactive landscape-scale fuel treatments in remote wilderness, precisely the conditions the WHFB plan targets through year-round herbivory at low public cost.
A visible positive signal from Interior—such as an announcement that the Department was evaluating or piloting elements of the plan, directing a review of holding-cost reductions through wilderness deployment, or highlighting the dual benefit to ranchers and wildfire risk—would have supplied the mirror-image late-cycle message to the constituencies alienated by Order 3454.
For wild-horse advocates who track BLM actions closely, it would have offered a non-lethal pathway that keeps horses on the landscape in a working role rather than accelerating removals.
For broader wildlife and public-lands voters concerned about commercial prioritization, it would have demonstrated that the administration could deliver forage relief for ranchers and taxpayer savings without treating wild horses solely as a forage competitor.
For rural and Western voters sensitive to both ranching economics and catastrophic fire, it would have linked documented wildfire-smoke mortality, insurance costs, and range improvements in a single package.
Because the margins in several contests were measured in dozens to a few thousand votes, the same arithmetic that makes a modest defection among these groups potentially decisive also makes a modest retention or crossover among them potentially decisive.
Targeted dissemination through the same advocacy networks that would have amplified criticism of Order 3454 could have amplified a constructive alternative. The political upside would have been especially relevant in public-lands districts where outdoor recreation, wildlife values, and residual ranching interests coexist, allowing the administration to claim a win that simultaneously addressed rancher forage needs, taxpayer waste, and the public-health dimensions of wildfire smoke documented in peer-reviewed work and insurance-industry coverage.
The counterfactual is structurally consistent with the earlier argument: in races decided by very small absolute numbers, a concrete, visible signal on a high-intensity public-lands and wildlife issue can move marginal votes. A positive WHFB-oriented note before the midterms would have been the signal most likely to retain or attract the very constituencies that Order 3454 risked repelling.

text:
Pedro Carrasco (on the canvas) wins the WBC Lightweight Title that had been stripped from Ken Buchanan on June 25th, on November 5, 1971, with a 12th round DQ win over Mando Ramos in Madrid, Spain.

In front of disbelieving Spanish fans, Ramos, seemingly on the brink of a KO, was disqualified for a low blow with the Spaniard on the canvas.

Carrasco would become Spain's second world champion.

UPI would write in their report that "Carrasco himself was too dazed from the punishment handed out by Ramos in 11 rounds to fully realize that he had been proclaimed world champion."

"We feel shameful it was not Carrasco but an unfair referee (Samuel Obudate of Nigeria) who defeated Mando Ramos. But above such an injustice the overwhelming superiority of Ramos over Pedro Carrasco was clear and evident to everybody." said Fernando Vadillo, a Spanish reporter.

"It has been the greatest robbery in boxing's history. I had it won and knocked the Saniard down four times. He was finished. If I had won the fight the way he won it, I wouldn't feel like a champion. If he does not offer me a return fight, I'll never consider him a champ." -Mando Ramos

They would rematch in February of 1972 with Ramos regaining the title via 15-round split decision. This one just as controversial as the first as most unofficial scorers had Carrasco clearly winning the bout at the LA Sports Arena.

The WBC ordered an immediate 3rd fight between the two citing the fact that all 3 officials in this bout were from California. Knocked down in the 1st and 2nd rounds, Carrasco would lose a 15-round split decision in their third meeting.

After drinking a bottle of soda in his dressing room after the (3rd) bout, Ramos was given a post-fight urinalysis in which was found traces of Benzedrine. Unknowing if it was from the soda, WBC President Ramon Velasquez ordered a 4th bout between the two, to follow Ramos' signed defense against Chango Carmona of Mexico.

The 4th bout would never come off as Ramos would lose the title, in September of 1972, to Carmona via 8th round TKO at the LA Memorial Coliseum.

Ramos would go 4-5-1 following the title loss to Carmona finishing his career 37-11-1 with 23 KO wins.

Pedro Carrasco would win twice after losing this 3rd fight with Ramos, and retire with a remarkable record of 105-3-2 (67 KO wins).

The two losses to Ramos had followed an 8-year unbeaten streak for Carrasco.

After beginning his career 12–1–1, Carrasco had a streak in which he went 92–0–1. The draw came after Carrasco had won 83 consecutive fights. This undefeated streak was longer than Julio Cesar Chavez's (90–0–1). Chávez's streak, however, was from the beginning of the career, and he was 87–0 before the draw.

text:
We pay 15k/yr in property taxes alone, in addition to hundreds a month in municipal utilities. If that's not enough, that's not because it's a suburb. I promise you I could offer comparable service privately for a fraction of that, including infrastructure maintenance and schools. 

Frankly, I'd rather have my own power without the grid but I don't want to jump through the permitting hoops yet. I'd rather have our own RO filtered well water, but it's not allowed. We already have Starlink. And I wouldn't mind paying someone else to do pick up our trash weekly instead of the city -- it's not a small amount they're charging.

That leaves roads and schools. I'd be happy to switch to full on homeschooling (we're already at partial), so that just leaves roads. 

California charges 63c/gal in gas tax, presumably for road maintenance. At say 30mpg that works out to ~2c/mile. At a modest 5000 cars/day and 6000 days between repaving, that's $600k/mile for repaving, which happens to be enough. 

As for the 50ft of low traffic street in front of my house, I'd be more than happy to pay for its upkeep. I believe it would work out to a few hundred $ a year.

That leaves me wanting no services from my local government except records keeping, law enforcement, and firefighting. I feel pretty confident the first two aren't made more expensive by us living in a suburb, and if suburban firefighting is too onerous of an expense, I'd be quite willing to set up a self-serve solution for that. God knows it works far more effectively for rural communities in the California mountains to take firefighting into their own hands if they want to save their property. And if anything it's a lot easier in a suburb than in a rural or urban environment to do so.

text:
Jascha Sohl-Dickstein’s presentation at the "Physics and AI" conference held at Stanford University in June 2026 is a matter of record. His core advice: if one believes that AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) could arrive within a few years, the traditional "PhD–postdoc–tenure-track" trajectory should no longer be viewed as the default, safe path. Instead, researchers should integrate AI tools into their work as early as possible and select research topics that will remain valuable upon completion—specifically those that stand to gain further value as computational power scales. Regarding Anthropic’s IPO and valuation, it can be confirmed that the company filed its S-1 registration statement in October 2026; reports suggest it may seek to raise as much as $100 billion, with a potential valuation reaching $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion. While CEO Dario Amodei did predict that AI could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs, he also acknowledged that the timeline for this remains unverified by data. Furthermore, research from Anthropic itself indicates that in roles with the highest exposure to AI, hiring for workers aged 22 to 25 has declined by approximately 14%—rather than the jobs disappearing entirely.

Key Themes from Sohl-Dickstein’s Presentation

Titled "Advice for Young Researchers in the Early and Final Days of the Anthropocene," Sohl-Dickstein’s talk was delivered at the Stanford PAI26 conference in June 2026. His central argument rests on three exponential curves: over the past decade, the computational power used for AI training has increased by a factor of roughly 10 million; the time required for AI to independently complete software tasks—as tracked by METR—has grown tenfold in less than a year; and, over the last seven months or so, AI has begun to solve some of the open problems left by the mathematician Paul Erdős.

Based on these trends, he offers specific counsel to young researchers: ensure that your research topic will still be meaningful by the time it is completed—avoid the scenario where you "toil away for two years, only to find that someone else can achieve better results simply by prompting the latest foundational model." He also advises using AI tools early on for brainstorming, gathering feedback, and iterative analysis—but warns against outsourcing the drafting of initial texts, because "writing is thinking." He did not advise against pursuing a PhD; rather, he cautioned against viewing a PhD and a tenured faculty position as a "naturally safe option," suggesting that the risks inherent in the traditional academic path should be re-evaluated.

Anthropic’s IPO and Valuation: Verifiable Data

In October 2026, Anthropic filed a 335-page S-1 registration statement, planning an IPO on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT." Reports indicate that the offering could raise as much as $100 billion, surpassing the $860 billion record set by SpaceX in June 2026. The company was valued at $965 billion during a private funding round in early 2026, and its valuation could reach $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion following the IPO. Filings reveal that revenue for the first half of 2026 exceeded $16 billion, while the net loss reached $80.7 billion—a significant increase from the $13 billion loss recorded during the same period the previous year.

Amodei’s Employment Forecasts: Original Statements and Data

In 2025, Dario Amodei predicted that AI could eliminate more than 50% of entry-level white-collar jobs within five years. In an October 2026 interview with Bloomberg, he stated that he remained "just as concerned," though he declined to provide updated figures, acknowledging, "I don’t know exactly." He described a mechanism he calls a "productivity hump": after 90% of a job is automated, the remaining 10% allows a worker to become ten times more efficient—but "eventually, it approaches 100%," at which point the tasks themselves vanish, leaving no work for humans to perform.

However, research conducted by Anthropic itself in March 2026 indicated that its AI model, Claude, currently covers approximately 33% of tasks within computer and mathematics-related fields, with a theoretical upper limit of 94%. Among occupations with the highest exposure to AI, hiring for workers aged 22 to 25 declined by about 14%, yet there has been no systemic rise in unemployment. Furthermore, as of the end of 2025, the Yale Budget Lab had not identified any significant macroeconomic impact of AI on the labor market. An October 2026 report from *The Guardian* cites experts who question an Anthropic report on how AI is transforming the nature of work, suggesting it was "written from the perspective of a company looking to sell its stock."

Assessment

Jascha Sohl-Dickstein’s advice is not intended to "derail a plan," but rather to encourage young researchers to re-evaluate the assumptions underlying their long-term career paths in light of rapidly evolving technological capabilities. While this advice comes from an Anthropic scientist—and Anthropic’s IPO valuation does indeed hinge on investor belief that AI will replace a significant portion of human labor—this tension is real. However, verifiable data indicates that the impact of AI on entry-level employment currently manifests as a "14% decline in hiring" rather than a "50% disappearance of jobs"—a trend that, notably, began to worsen even before the release of ChatGPT. For students, utilizing AI tools and pursuing a formal degree are not mutually exclusive; Sohl-Dickstein himself explicitly advocates for using AI tools while maintaining independent judgment, rather than abandoning systematic training.

text:
Everyone says short cold emails work better, including me.

But if you're going to spend the time researching a prospect, a LONG cold email can work.

Here's how a sales rep at Ramp did it correctly:

• He opens with "I have a quick wager." That line alone makes the prospect want to read the rest.

• Then he keeps him reading with something he cares about: his college's next game. (Digging up a detail like that is EXACTLY the kind of research I'd hand to AI, the rest should stay with the rep)

• Talking about someone's interests is usually a waste of words in an email. It works here because he turns it into a bet: if Clemson wins, the prospect gives him 20 minutes. If Syracuse wins, he buys the prospect's next lunch.

• Whichever way the bet goes, they end up talking about Ramp. So he introduces Ramp in 1 sentence with MASSIVE social proof: over $1.5B raised from Goldman Sachs, Citi, Stripe and Founders Fund.

• He ends on what Ramp's free platform does, then ties it back to the bet: "Anything to lose by giving us a look?"

So the email sounds human, uses curiosity, does something unique AND shows he did his research.

All of this while still doing everything a cold email should do: make your offer, drop social proof, give an easy yes and a dream outcome.

Absolute masterclass.

text:
Tech Crashes. Oil Rebounds. Payrolls Are Next. | November 6, 2026
📍Data From https://t.co/rtKhA53pFF Daily Report

Wednesday: celebrate election clarity.
Thursday: question the entire AI spending trade.
That was an expensive change of mind.

Wall Street’s post-election relief rally reversed sharply as investors reassessed what a Democratic sweep could mean for data center expansion, semiconductor demand and infrastructure financing.
🔻 Dow: approximately −3.4%
🔻 S&P 500: −4.36%
🔻 Nasdaq: approximately −5.5%
🔻 Philadelphia Semiconductor Index: approximately −12%

SanDisk plunged roughly 22%. Micron and AMD lost around 17%. Nvidia dropped about 9%.

All 11 S&P 500 sectors declined. The damage had spread beyond a narrow chip-stock correction.

1️⃣ Lower yields offered little protection from falling earnings confidence.
Treasuries rallied, with short-term yields falling more sharply than longer-term yields.
That distinction matters. Falling yields can support equity valuations when inflation cools without damaging growth. They offer less comfort when investors are simultaneously questioning future revenues, project execution and financing capacity.
Thursday’s message: a lower discount rate cannot automatically rescue a deteriorating earnings narrative.

2️⃣ AI regulation fears are becoming a spending-timing trade.

The immediate concern is whether greater scrutiny of electricity costs, permitting and data center construction will delay deployment.

For suppliers, revenue pushed further into the future can justify a lower valuation today. For leveraged operators, delays can be particularly painful because financing costs continue while expected cash receipts move back.

But political risk still needs to be separated from confirmed commercial damage. An election result does not automatically cancel an existing order.

Watch customer guidance, construction schedules and credit conditions for evidence.

3️⃣ Oil’s rebound keeps inflation risk alive.

Crude recovered roughly 3–4%, while gold advanced.

That combination complicates the comforting idea that weaker technology stocks will simply lead to easier monetary policy. Persistent energy pressure could limit how quickly central banks respond to deteriorating growth expectations.

The Bank of England illustrated that tension by raising its policy rate 25 basis points to 4%, with one policymaker preferring a larger increase.

4️⃣ Tonight’s payrolls report could change the next trade.

🕘 21:30 UTC+8 / 08:30 EST

Consensus:
• Nonfarm payrolls: +65,000
• Unemployment rate: 4.2%

A moderate employment rebound with contained wage growth could help stabilize sentiment.

A strong jobs-and-wages combination could revive tightening concerns. A severe employment disappointment could deepen growth fears—even if bond yields fall further.

Read payrolls alongside wages, unemployment and revisions. One headline cannot settle all four questions.

After a selloff this large, a rebound is possible. Its durability will depend on whether semiconductor leadership, market breadth and financing conditions actually improve.

“Stocks are cheaper” is an observation. It still needs a trading thesis.

text:
I started WiseXBet with almost nothing. At one point, I was running out of money before the platform even had games.

I spent weeks reaching out to game aggregators in different countries, trying to convince them to work with us without charging setup fees. Most never replied. Eventually, one guy from Russia took a chance on us.

The tech side was another battle.

The entire platform was built by an Indian team I'm still working with today. I had to convince their owner to believe in me and take a risk on this project, even though I couldn't offer anything close to the budget a platform like this normally requires.

No big office. No massive investment. No big industry connections.

Just a room in Tunisia, a lot of persistence, and a belief that we could actually build this.

We're still fighting to make it work.

Looking back, I think the hardest part of building something from nothing isn't the technology or the money.

It's convincing people to believe in something before there's much to show them.

What's the biggest risk someone has ever taken on you?

text:
AFFIRM $AFRM — 34% GMV GROWTH IS IMPRESSIVE. BUT AI UNDERWRITING COULD BE THE BIGGER OPPORTUNITY.
What stood out to me from Affirm's earnings call wasn't just the revenue and earnings beat. It was how management is using AI to improve lending decisions while expanding into new payment channels.
CEO Max Levchin revealed that Affirm's new transformer-based underwriting model performed roughly twice as well as its next traditional model candidate in internal testing.
That doesn't mean twice as many approvals. Management believes it could increase approval rates by 2–3 percentage points without incremental credit losses.
For a company targeting at least 30% GMV growth in FY27, that's potentially significant.
THREE THINGS I'M WATCHING
🔹 AI underwriting: Better risk assessment could unlock additional transaction volume without sacrificing credit quality.
🔹 Agentic commerce: Affirm wants AI shopping agents to compare financing offers alongside product prices. Around 1M SKUs already have brand-funded promotions in its app, although agentic monetisation remains early.
🔹 Distribution: Affirm Card, digital wallets and merchant partnerships are expanding where consumers can use its financing products.
BUT THE CREDIT QUESTION MATTERS
Management acknowledged higher provisions, partly linked to controlled underwriting experiments.
Affirm's short-duration loans and fixed-rate funding provide some flexibility, but neither eliminates the risk of rising delinquencies or weaker consumer spending.
MY TAKE
I'm constructive on Affirm's growth trajectory.
The combination of better underwriting, broader distribution and improving transaction economics could make this a more profitable business as it scales.
But I want to see the AI underwriting improvements reflected in sustained credit performance, not just higher approval rates.
Growing GMV by 30%+ is impressive. Growing it without proportionately increasing credit losses is what could create lasting shareholder value.

text:
Here is Sweden's greatest love poem; Grok's English translation follows.

DEN NYA SKAPELSEN ELLER INBILLNINGENS VÄRLD  

Johan Henric Kellgren (1790)

Du, som af skönhet och behagen  
en ren och himmelsk urbild ger!  
Jag såg dig — och från denna dagen  
jag endast dig i världen ser.  

Död låg naturen för mitt öga,  
djupt låg hon för min känsla död —  
kom så en fläkt ifrån det höga  
och ljus och lif i världen böd.  

Och ljuset kom, och lifvet tändes,  
en själ i stela massan flöt;  
allt tog ett anletsdrag som kändes,  
en röst som till mitt hjärta bröt.  

Kring rymden nya himlar sträcktes,  
och jorden nya skrudar drog,  
och bildningen och snillet väcktes,  
och skönheten stod upp och log.  

Då fann min själ sig himlaburen,  
sig sprungen af en gudastam,  
och såg de under i naturen,  
som aldrig visheten förnam.  

Ej endast storhet och förmåga  
och glans och rymd och rörelse;  
ej blott i dalens djup det låga,  
och endast höjd i klipporne;  

men liflig till mitt öra fördes  
de höga sfärers harmoni;  
på berget änglars harpor hördes,  
ur djupet mörka andars skri.  

På fältet logo fridens löjen,  
skräck omsmög i den skumma dal,  
och lunden hviskade om nöjen,  
och skogen suckade om kval;  

och vrede var i hafvets vågor,  
och ömhet uti källans sus,  
och majestät i solens lågor,  
och blygsamhet i månans ljus.  

Hämnd gick att blixtens pilar hvässa,  
mod skakade orkanens arm,  
och cedern lyftade en hjässa,  
och blomman öppnade en barm. —  

O lefvande förstånd af tingen!  
O snillets, känslans hemlighet!  
Hvem fattade dig, Skönhet? — Ingen  
förutan den som älska vet.  

För mig, när du naturen målar  
till himlar utaf ljus och väl,  
hvad är du? — Återbrutna strålar  
af *Hilmas* bild uti min själ.  

Hon är det i min själ, hvars stämpel  
till skapelsen förtjusning bär;  
och jorden uppstod till ett tempel,  
där hon gudomligheten är.  

Du, som af skönhet och behagen  
en ren och himmelsk urbild ger!  
Jag såg dig — och från denna dagen  
jag endast dig i världen ser.  

I allt din lånta teckning kännes,  
o evigt samma, evigt ny!  
Din växt blef liljans växt, och hennes  
den friska glansen af din hy.  

Din blick i dagens blickar blandas,  
din röst fick näktergalens sång,  
jag dig i rosens vällukt andas,  
och västanfläkten har din gång.  

Ej nog — du själfva fasan gläder,  
du fyller afgrundar med ljus;  
du öknarne i blomster kläder,  
och tjusar i ruiners grus.  

Och när min tanka hänryckt vimlar  
och flyr, och söker trängtande,  
och söker genom jord och himlar  
det sälla stoftets skapare,  

och frågar, i hvad skepnad fattas,  
att, öm och god och glad och mild,  
vår högsta dyrkan värdig skattas, —  
då visas han mig i din bild.  

I kungars slott, i hof och städer  
jag ser bland tusende blott dig;  
och när min fot i hyddan träder,  
är du där redan före mig.  

Jag gick att visdomsdjupet spörja;  
din tanka ref mig ur dess famn.  
Jag gick att hjältars kväden börja;  
men cittran lärde blott ditt namn.  

Jag ville ärans höjder hinna,  
men bortvek i det fjät du gick.  
Jag ville lyckans skatter finna,  
och fann dem alla i din blick.  

Du, som af skönhet och behagen  
en ren och himmelsk urbild ger!  
Jag såg dig — och från denna dagen  
jag endast dig i världen ser.  

Förgäfves ur din åsyn tagen,  
mig blott din tanka unnas mer:  
i dina spår af minnet dragen,  
jag endast dig i världen ser.

English Translation

You who of beauty and grace  
give a pure and heavenly archetype!  
I saw you — and from that day  
I see only you in the world.  

Nature lay dead before my eye,  
deeply she lay dead to my feeling —  
then came a breath from on high  
and offered light and life to the world.  

And the light came, and life was kindled,  
a soul flowed into the rigid mass;  
everything took on a recognizable face,  
a voice that broke through to my heart.  

Around space new heavens stretched,  
and the earth put on new raiment,  
and culture and genius were awakened,  
and beauty stood up and smiled.  

Then my soul found itself heaven-borne,  
sprung from a divine lineage,  
and saw the wonders in nature  
that wisdom never perceived.  

Not only greatness and power  
and splendor and space and motion;  
not merely the low in the valley’s depth,  
and height only in the cliffs;  

but vividly to my ear were brought  
the high spheres’ harmony;  
on the mountain angels’ harps were heard,  
from the deep dark spirits’ cries.  

On the field peace’s smiles laughed,  
terror crept about in the dim valley,  
and the grove whispered of pleasures,  
and the forest sighed of torments;  

and wrath was in the sea’s waves,  
and tenderness in the spring’s murmur,  
and majesty in the sun’s flames,  
and modesty in the moon’s light.  

Vengeance went to whet the lightning’s arrows,  
courage shook the hurricane’s arm,  
and the cedar lifted a brow,  
and the flower opened a bosom. —  

O living understanding of things!  
O secret of genius, of feeling!  
Who comprehended you, Beauty? — None  
except the one who knows how to love.  

For me, when you paint nature  
into heavens of light and well-being,  
what are you? — Refracted rays  
of *Hilma’s* image in my soul.  

She is that in my soul whose stamp  
bears the enchantment of creation;  
and the earth arose as a temple  
where she is the divinity.  

You who of beauty and grace  
give a pure and heavenly archetype!  
I saw you — and from that day  
I see only you in the world.  

In everything your borrowed outline is recognized,  
O eternally the same, eternally new!  
Your form became the lily’s form, and hers  
the fresh gleam of your complexion.  

Your gaze mingles in the day’s glances,  
your voice took the nightingale’s song,  
I breathe you in the rose’s fragrance,  
and the west wind has your gait.  

Not enough — you delight even terror,  
you fill abysses with light;  
you clothe the deserts in flowers,  
and charm amid the rubble of ruins.  

And when my thought, enraptured, swarms  
and flees, and seeks urgently,  
and seeks through earth and heavens  
the Creator of that blessed dust,  

and asks in what form is assumed  
that, tender and good and glad and mild,  
is deemed worthy of our highest worship —  
then he is shown to me in your image.  

In kings’ palaces, in courts and cities  
I see among thousands only you;  
and when my foot enters the cottage,  
you are already there before me.  

I went to question the depths of wisdom;  
your thought tore me from its embrace.  
I went to begin heroes’ songs;  
but the lute taught only your name.  

I wished to reach the heights of honor,  
but turned aside in the track you walked.  
I wished to find fortune’s treasures,  
and found them all in your glance.  

You who of beauty and grace  
give a pure and heavenly archetype!  
I saw you — and from that day  
I see only you in the world.  

In vain taken from your sight,  
only your thought is granted me more:  
drawn by memory in your tracks,  
I see only you in the world.

text:
APHA’s Selective Outrage: When Public Health Leadership Turns a Blind Eye to Jewish Concerns

An Editorial on Dr. Georges Benjamin, Abdul El-Sayed, and the Credibility of the American Public Health Association

There is something profoundly contradictory about the American Public Health Association publicly celebrating Dr. Abdul El-Sayed as “respectful” and someone who “follows the evidence wherever it goes,” while overlooking a documented record of rhetoric and political associations that have deeply troubled members of Michigan’s Jewish community.

Apparently, the evidence Dr. Georges Benjamin so enthusiastically celebrates managed to travel everywhere except through the Jewish community’s front door.

Consider the record.

In March 2026, following a violent attack on Temple Israel, a Michigan synagogue and childcare center, El-Sayed invoked the phrase “hurt people hurt people” while discussing the attacker. Jewish leaders condemned the response as insensitive and potentially excusing antisemitic violence. 

El-Sayed also campaigned alongside Hasan Piker, whose inflammatory commentary about Israel and American Jews drew condemnation from Jewish leaders and prominent Democrats. Piker’s suggestion that certain rhetoric by American Jews could provoke violence against them was especially disturbing. The controversy raised legitimate questions about the responsibility of candidates and government officials who elevate divisive political personalities.

Meanwhile, Michigan rabbis publicly objected to El-Sayed’s characterization of Israeli government conduct as “bloodthirsty,” warning that such language could reinforce longstanding antisemitic stereotypes. A coalition of Jewish leaders subsequently demanded clearer commitments to Jewish safety, identity, self-determination, and political inclusion.

These are not imaginary grievances manufactured by political opponents. Jewish religious leaders and community members, including progressive Democrats, have raised these documented concerns.

El-Sayed’s rhetoric continues to alienate Jewish Americans who have raised legitimate concerns, reducing their fears to political inconveniences, their objections to disposable grievances, and their dignity to collateral damage in a grotesque spectacle of selective inclusion.

And therein lies the problem with APHA’s promotional spectacle.

The APHA’s own Code of Conduct emphasizes respect, fairness, honesty, inclusion, and sensitivity to religious identity. Yet its CEO has offered an unqualified character testimonial without acknowledging the substantial controversy surrounding the very qualities he celebrates.

Since when did public health leadership become an exercise in selective listening, where the experiences of an affected minority become inconvenient footnotes to a preferred political narrative?

Dr. Benjamin is entitled to praise El-Sayed’s scientific credentials, healthcare experience, and professional accomplishments. But scientific expertise is not a certificate of ethical infallibility, and electoral victory is not absolution from public accountability.

Public health demands more than polished endorsements and inspirational slogans. It demands cultural humility, honest communication, consistent ethical standards, and respect for communities that report feeling excluded or threatened.

The question for APHA is not whether Abdul El-Sayed deserves professional recognition. It is why its leadership chose unqualified praise when the documented record called for greater nuance, transparency, and sensitivity.

An institution that champions evidence should not appear to cherry-pick it. An organization devoted to inclusion should not make Jewish Americans wonder whether their concerns count.

That contradiction deserves an answer from Dr. Benjamin. And left unaddressed, it risks becoming a stain on APHA’s institutional credibility.

References

1. Associated Press (August 29, 2026). El-Sayed apologizes for comments following Michigan synagogue attack.

2. Associated Press (August 24, 2026). El-Sayed distances himself from Hasan Piker’s comments about Israel and American Jews.

3. Michigan Public (September 9, 2026). Jewish faith leaders air concerns with Democratic Senate nominee El-Sayed.

4. Michigan Public (October 29, 2026). Jewish voters divided over Abdul El-Sayed.

5. American Public Health Association. APHA Code of Conduct.
