text:
LAKEWOOD CHARTER SCHOOL FACES FEDERAL LAWSUIT AFTER TEACHER REPORTS RACIST THREATS AGAINST STUDENTS

LAKEWOOD, COLORADO | NOVEMBER 5, 2026

A former teacher at Addenbrooke Classical Academy in Lakewood has filed a federal lawsuit alleging he was fired after reporting racist graffiti, threats of sexual violence, and disturbing references to a slave auction involving students of color.

The allegations raise serious questions about student safety, discrimination, and whether school employees can report misconduct without facing retaliation.

According to a November 5 report from FOX31, Nicholas Newman, the school’s former choir director, was terminated on May 20, 2025, just 18 days after learning about the graffiti and subsequently reporting it to school officials and Colorado’s Safe2Tell program.

WHAT THE LAWSUIT ALLEGES

On May 2, 2025, Newman reportedly learned about graffiti inside a school restroom containing racial slurs, threats of sexual violence, and references to a slave auction.

The graffiti allegedly identified five male students of color by name.

The lawsuit also accuses Addenbrooke Classical Academy of tolerating homophobic language and maintaining a hostile environment for LGBTQ+ students and employees.

These allegations extend beyond offensive language. They involve reported threats directed at identifiable children inside an educational institution responsible for protecting them.

THE REPORT AND TERMINATION

According to the lawsuit, Newman initially reported the incident to school administrators before submitting a report to Colorado’s Safe2Tell program on May 4.

Safe2Tell is designed to allow students and community members to report threats and safety concerns, including anonymously.

On May 15, Newman alleges school administrators confronted him about his report and offered him two options: resign or return to work under increased scrutiny.

Five days later, on May 20, he was fired.

According to the reporting, Newman had been invited to return for the following school year only weeks before his termination.

The timing of those events is central to his retaliation allegations.

A SECOND LAWSUIT

FOX31 also reports that a separate lawsuit filed on behalf of a former student of color references the same racist graffiti incident from May 2025.

That means the alleged conduct is now the subject of litigation involving both a former employee and a former student.

The claims in those lawsuits have not been established as fact by a court.

THE SCHOOL RESPONDS

Addenbrooke Classical Academy disputes Newman’s allegations.

In a statement provided through its public relations representatives, the school said it takes allegations of discrimination, harassment, and retaliation seriously.

The academy specifically denied that Newman was terminated for raising concerns about discrimination.

School officials acknowledged that offensive and racist graffiti was discovered in a restroom in April 2025.

According to the school, administrators restricted access to the restroom, interviewed multiple students, and addressed the male student body about appropriate behavior and respect for others.

The school said its investigation did not identify those responsible.

Administrators maintain that steps were taken to prevent students from being further exposed to the graffiti.

The academy also said it encourages students, families, and employees to report discrimination and harassment without fear of retaliation.

Citing ongoing litigation and employee confidentiality, the school declined to comment further.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT

Newman’s federal lawsuit names Addenbrooke Classical Academy, Principal John Byrne, and former Executive Director Ric Netzer.

He is seeking lost wages, damages, and attorney’s fees.

The court will ultimately determine whether the evidence supports his claims.

But the allegations raise questions that deserve public scrutiny.

How does a school respond when students are allegedly targeted by racist threats of sexual violence?

What protections exist for teachers who report those threats outside the school’s administration?

And how can parents be confident that reporting serious safety concerns will lead to meaningful action rather than retaliation?

A reporting system is only effective when people trust that using it will not put their education, employment, or safety at risk.

The allegations are particularly concerning because the graffiti reportedly identified specific students of color, while the school’s own statement acknowledges that investigators did not identify the people responsible.

Students deserve to attend school without being subjected to racist threats. Employees deserve to raise concerns about student safety without fear of unlawful retaliation.

Whether that protection was violated in this case is now a matter for the federal courts.

Source: FOX31 KDVR, reporting by Victoria Garnes, November 5, 2026.

text:
𝗕𝘂𝗿𝗴𝘂𝗺’𝘀 𝗕𝗹𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿
There is a coherent, if speculative, argument that DOI Sec. Burgum’s Order 3454 could have cost Republicans votes in a subset of close races—particularly in Western or public-lands-adjacent districts—through the mechanism of motivated, single-issue or multi-issue voters who already viewed federal public-lands policy as tilted too far toward commercial extraction.
Opinion By: Capt. William E. Simpson II - USMM Ret. - Rancher-Wild Horse Researcher
The case rests on existing opinion data, the size and intensity of certain constituencies, the narrow margins in several contests, and the order’s explicit prioritization of livestock over other uses. It does not rest on any direct polling that tested the order itself due to a short window between Burgum’s announcement of the Order (Oct. 28th) and Nov. 3rd, 2026.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗹𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗲𝗻𝘃𝗶𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
Polling on public lands consistently shows broad, often bipartisan concern about management that prioritizes commercial or extractive uses over wildlife, recreation, and long-term ecological condition. Center for Western Priorities and Colorado College State of the Rockies surveys in recent cycles have found majorities (frequently 70–85%+) in Mountain West states viewing rollbacks of wildlife and land protections as a serious problem, and large majorities preferring to keep public lands in public hands rather than expand commercial access at the expense of other values. Opposition to treating public lands primarily as a revenue stream for a narrow set of interests is not fringe; it appears across party lines when the question is framed around wildlife, open space, or local recreation access.Wild-horse constituencies amplify this. Advocacy organizations, online communities, and adoption/rescue networks have built a durable, emotionally engaged audience that treats roundups, fertility control, and forage allocation as core issues. While the absolute number of pure single-issue wild-horse voters is smaller than the broader public-lands or wildlife electorate, these voters are high-intensity: they track BLM and Interior actions closely, share information rapidly, and have demonstrated willingness to contact officials and mobilize around specific policy moves.
Order 3454’s language directing accelerated reductions of wild horses and burros “to the maximum extent practicable,” tracking of fertility-control treatments ($30-million to be spent on using an EPA registered pesticide, PZP, to sterilize wild horses) and progress toward AML to free forage for livestock maps directly onto the priorities this group has long opposed.
𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝘃𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀
The theoretical pathway is straightforward:• Order 3454 was framed by its supporters as helping ranchers, cutting red tape, and using managed grazing for wildfire reduction. Critics (including wild-horse and some wildlife groups) described it as a systematic elevation of livestock AUMs above wildlife, native predators, and free-roaming equines, with concrete directives to expand grazing, reinstate suspended AUMs, and accelerate horse reductions.
For voters already inclined to see public-lands policy as captured by commercial interests, the order supplied a fresh, high-profile confirmation issued by a Cabinet secretary one week before Election Day.
• In close races, the relevant voters need not be large in absolute numbers. Margins measured in dozens to a few thousand votes (as reported in several Senate and House contests) mean that even a modest number of motivated defectors, lower-intensity Republicans who stayed home, or independent/crossover voters who shifted can decide the outcome. A subset of these voters may treat public-lands and wildlife issues as secondary but still salient enough to tip a decision when other factors are close.
• The one-week window limited mass-media penetration, but it is long enough for targeted dissemination. Advocacy networks, Substack writers, social-media accounts focused on public lands or wild horses, and local conservation groups can move information to their existing audiences faster than general news cycles. Voters who already follow these channels would have seen the order framed as an attack on wildlife and wild horses rather than as a rancher-support measure.
𝗦𝗰𝗼𝗽𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗴𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
This mechanism is most plausible in districts or states with meaningful public-lands acreage, outdoor-recreation economies, or visible wild-horse populations (parts of the Mountain West, certain rural or exurban districts elsewhere). It is less plausible as a decisive factor in urban or Eastern races where public lands are abstract. It also competes with larger, longer-running drivers—cost of living, the Middle East conflict and energy prices, overall presidential approval—that dominated most post-election analysis.
The order’s own framing around wildfire mitigation and domestic meat production could have neutralized or even attracted some ranching-community or rural voters who prioritize those https://t.co/WycajsAD5v short, the argument is that Order 3454 supplied a concrete, late-cycle signal of commercial prioritization on public lands to constituencies that already held strong views on the issue and that, in races decided by very small absolute numbers of votes, even a limited mobilization or defection effect among those constituencies could have been enough to flip the result.
Whether that actually occurred in any specific race remains unmeasured; the absence of direct polling does not disprove the possibility, but it also means the claim stays in the realm of plausible mechanism rather than demonstrated causation.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹: 𝗮 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗪𝗛𝗙𝗕 𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗱𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
The same opinion environment and the same narrow margins create a symmetrical argument for the opposite outcome. Had Brenda Younkin (Deputy Assistant Secretary for Lands and Minerals Management), after receiving and reviewing the materials forwarded through Will Boothby in the May 13, 2026 email chain, briefed Secretary Burgum on the Wild Horse Fire Brigade (WHFB) plan and secured a public, affirmative administration statement or pilot commitment before Election Day, the same high-intensity public-lands, wildlife, and wild-horse constituencies could have been moved in the Republican direction.
The plan, as outlined in the March 11, 2026 correspondence and subsequent materials, proposes relocating excess horses (via existing authorities such as the Humane Transfer of Excess Animals Act and BLM IM-2022-035) into remote wilderness areas unsuited for commercial livestock, where natural predation maintains population stability; reducing fine fuels that drive catastrophic wildfire and toxic smoke; freeing forage on conflict allotments for ranchers; and addressing the public-health burden of wildfire smoke.
It is framed as legal under current statute, beneficial to livestock producers under FLPMA multiple-use principles, protective of wild-horse genetics and cultural heritage, and aligned with both wildfire mitigation and taxpayer savings.Independent reporting and data support core elements of that framing.
AM Best’s March 2026 podcast interviewed William Simpson specifically on novel toxins from super-hot wildfires, the public-health and insurance risks, and the cost of holding horses versus deploying them for fuel reduction, citing the roughly $150 million annual off-range holding figure.
NPR covered the same proposal to use BLM-held horses for wildfire mitigation rather than long-term captivity.
Epoch Times, Reasons to be Cheerful, Arizona Highways, OPB, and other outlets have reported on Simpson’s multi-year immersion observations (including the 2018 Klamathon Fire) and the plan’s logic.
On the underlying numbers: Congressional Research Service, E&E News/POLITICO, and BLM’s own data confirm that off-range holding routinely consumes $100–109 million per year—roughly two-thirds of the program’s $142–153 million budget—for tens of thousands of animals. UCLA’s 2024 Science Advances study (Connolly et al.) estimated 52,480–55,710 premature deaths in California alone from wildfire-smoke PM2.5 between 2008 and 2018, with an associated economic impact of $432–456 billion; broader U.S. analyses have placed annual attributable deaths in the low-to-mid tens of thousands.
The Klamathon Fire (July 5–21, 2018) burned 38,008 acres in Siskiyou County, California, according to contemporaneous incident reports and Wikipedia. Simpson served nine days as an unpaid local-knowledge technical advisor to CAL FIRE commanders. Multiple independent outlets (NPR, OPB, Arizona Highways) reported his first-hand observations that areas previously grazed by the local herd (estimated at roughly 5,000 acres of moderated fuels in some accounts) limited fire intensity, provided safer staging zones for personnel and equipment, and helped prevent advance into the Cascade-Siskiyou National Monument. These accounts describe horses remaining calm and continuing to graze near the fire front rather than panicking.
USFS budget trends further contextualize the cost argument.
Multiple analyses (including Forest Service reports cited by Wildfire Today and Taxpayer Network fact sheets) document that fire suppression and preparedness have grown to dominate the agency’s discretionary appropriations—rising from roughly 16% in 1995 to more than 50% in recent years when wildfire adjustment funds are included—while hazardous-fuels reduction, forest management, and prevention remain substantially smaller line items.
Salaries and expenses constitute a large share across accounts.
This allocation structure leaves limited resources for proactive landscape-scale fuel treatments in remote wilderness, precisely the conditions the WHFB plan targets through year-round herbivory at low public cost.
A visible positive signal from Interior—such as an announcement that the Department was evaluating or piloting elements of the plan, directing a review of holding-cost reductions through wilderness deployment, or highlighting the dual benefit to ranchers and wildfire risk—would have supplied the mirror-image late-cycle message to the constituencies alienated by Order 3454.
For wild-horse advocates who track BLM actions closely, it would have offered a non-lethal pathway that keeps horses on the landscape in a working role rather than accelerating removals.
For broader wildlife and public-lands voters concerned about commercial prioritization, it would have demonstrated that the administration could deliver forage relief for ranchers and taxpayer savings without treating wild horses solely as a forage competitor.
For rural and Western voters sensitive to both ranching economics and catastrophic fire, it would have linked documented wildfire-smoke mortality, insurance costs, and range improvements in a single package.
Because the margins in several contests were measured in dozens to a few thousand votes, the same arithmetic that makes a modest defection among these groups potentially decisive also makes a modest retention or crossover among them potentially decisive.
Targeted dissemination through the same advocacy networks that would have amplified criticism of Order 3454 could have amplified a constructive alternative. The political upside would have been especially relevant in public-lands districts where outdoor recreation, wildlife values, and residual ranching interests coexist, allowing the administration to claim a win that simultaneously addressed rancher forage needs, taxpayer waste, and the public-health dimensions of wildfire smoke documented in peer-reviewed work and insurance-industry coverage.
The counterfactual is structurally consistent with the earlier argument: in races decided by very small absolute numbers, a concrete, visible signal on a high-intensity public-lands and wildlife issue can move marginal votes. A positive WHFB-oriented note before the midterms would have been the signal most likely to retain or attract the very constituencies that Order 3454 risked repelling.

Missing teen allegedly forced to remove braces with pliers. 

A Utah teenager missing for more than 17 months has been found alive in Oregon, and new details from federal court documents outline what she allegedly endured during that time. Kylie Arellano, now 17, disappeared from Garden City, Utah, on May 29, 2025, when she was 15. She was rescued on November 1, 2026, from a home in Huntington, Oregon, after a tip that began with another player on the online game Among Us.

According to the New York Post and other reporting that reviewed the federal complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Utah, 39-year-old Adam Hunter Harmel is charged with transporting a minor across state lines with the intent to engage in criminal explicit activity. The documents allege he confined her to the basement of his home, where they shared a bed, kept a knife under his pillow, and made her sleep against the wall to prevent her from leaving. He allegedly became violent and forced her to remove her braces with pliers so she would be harder to identify. 

The complaint further states he met her online in May 2025, claimed a disability involving his hips, offered money, drove to Perry, Utah, to pick her up, and threw her phone into a river in Logan Canyon before taking her to Oregon. 

Harmel is presumed innocent until proven guilty in court.

text:
The brazen murder of Benjamin “Bugsy” Siegel remains one of the most infamous unsolved crimes in Mob history, blurring the lines between fact, speculation and conspiracy.

On June 20, 1947, Siegel was gunned down inside a Beverly Hills mansion. His murder made headlines nationwide, fueling decades of speculation about who pulled the trigger and why. Nearly 80 years later, the mystery remains unsolved.

But another intriguing part of Siegel’s story has remained largely hidden from public view: items recovered from his pockets following his murder.
Held in police evidence custody for nearly eight decades, these remarkable artifacts offer a rare and personal glimpse into the life of one of America’s most notorious mobsters.

Among the items are a wallet-sized photograph of Siegel’s girlfriend, Virginia Hill, with a handwritten love note on the back; childhood photographs of his daughters, Barbara and Millicent; a photograph of both daughters as teenagers; a business card belonging to his longtime friend and criminal associate, Meyer Lansky; and a handwritten note containing information about the Beverly Hills home where Siegel was murdered.

The collection’s public debut follows a decades-long effort to recover these belongings from police custody. Following his death at age 41, the Beverly Hills Police Department retained the items as evidence in its investigation. In 2025, Siegel’s granddaughter, Wendy Rosen, filed a lawsuit seeking their return to the family. After a judge ordered their release, The Mob Museum acquired the collection from Rosen.

Beginning Friday, Nov. 13, these never-before-displayed artifacts will be on public view at The Mob Museum, offering an intimate glimpse into Siegel’s personal life and the final chapter of one of organized crime’s most enduring mysteries.

text:
Why SpaceX can be a better stock than Nvidia:
Nvidia is the pure-play leader in AI chips ,
extremely strong, but concentrated. 
Almost all its value rides on one cycle: GPU demand for training and inference.

SpaceX is broader and more diversified:

•  Multiple high-growth engines: Rockets/launch, Starlink (broadband + direct-to-cell), and a rapidly scaling AI business (Grok, Colossus, orbital compute ambitions). AI already contributed a large share of recent revenue.

•  Physical AI stack: It combines compute, connectivity, launch capacity, and (via Tesla synergies) robots and autonomy. Nvidia supplies the chips; SpaceX aims to own more of the full stack that uses them.

•  Recurring revenue + optionality: Starlink is a high-margin subscription business. On top of that you get long-term optionality on space infrastructure, humanoid robotics, and off-world applications that Nvidia doesn’t have.

•  Less single-cycle risk: If the current AI chip boom cools or competition intensifies, Nvidia feels it directly. SpaceX has other cash-generating businesses that can underwrite continued AI investment.

•  Integrated “fund” profile: One stock gives exposure to space, connectivity, frontier AI, and physical robotics/autonomy, something no pure semiconductor company offers.

Caveat: Nvidia still has clearer near-term dominance, higher margins in its core business, and less execution risk on ambitious multi-front plans. SpaceX’s edge is diversification, vertical integration, and multi-decade optionality rather than pure AI-chip concentration.

text:
The New York Times: Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday dismissed reports that he was planning to leave the Trump administration and declined to answer questions about his political future. Working for President Trump until the end of his term has “always been my plan,” he said in an interview with The New York Times.

Responding to the news reports that he was mulling an exit, Mr. Rubio said, “I don’t know where these things come from, to be honest with you.”

“I love the work I’m doing,” he continued. “And plus I always laugh when they say he’s going to leave his job. I go, ‘Which one?’”

Mr. Rubio, who is also Mr. Trump’s national security adviser, declined to answer questions about whether he was considering running for president in 2028.

“I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore,” he said in the interview, in his White House office. “I just won’t do it.”

Mr. Rubio has said that he would support Vice President JD Vance if he ran for president.

“JD is a very good friend of mine,” he told NBC News in May. “If JD runs for president, I think he’d be a phenomenal candidate. I’ve said publicly, and I’ll say it again, I’ll be the first person to sign up and support him.”

Mr. Vance offered a striking critique in his post-election analysis on Wednesday in a lengthy post on social media, commentary that distanced himself from Mr. Trump. The vice president blamed the war with Iran for Republicans’ disastrous election results and said Republicans had turned against the administration’s policy on Israel and its messaging on the economy. The president has closely aligned himself with Israel and dismissed affordability concerns as a “hoax.”

Mr. Rubio initially deflected when asked whether he agreed with Mr. Vance’s assessment, saying he was not “really involved in domestic politics.”

But Mr. Trump brought Mr. Rubio onstage at his political rally on Sunday in Kansas and lavished praise on him, joking that he might have to fire him because he had become “too popular.” Mr. Rubio spoke briefly, praising Mr. Trump for keeping Americans safe.

Mr. Rubio explained why he was there, as the designated national security official traveling with the president, and then acknowledged that Mr. Trump had said the war was a factor in the elections.

“Higher prices at the gas pump, I acknowledge, is not like the kind of thing you campaign on and brag about,” he said.

But Mr. Rubio said Mr. Trump “deserves a tremendous amount of credit” for taking action that he thought was necessary even if it was not popular among voters.

“Ultimately, that is the price of leadership — is the willingness to do things that may not be politically popular or expedient but are necessary for your country and its long-term future,” he said.

I sat beside my son and raised my hand. I felt a little silly waving at a dog from two feet away.

He watched my fingers, then tipped his head to get a better look at the rest of me. When I shifted my weight, the sole of my shoe squeaked. My son looked down. The dog kept watching my face.

My wife came to find us. By then a volunteer had offered to bring him into the visiting room, so we spent another half hour on the floor, this time with a dog who had no interest in stealing anybody’s hat.

He liked having his chest scratched. When my wife stopped, he put a paw on her wrist. She started again. He took his paw back.

We asked the volunteer how he let you know he needed to go outside and how to wake him without startling him. Then I went back to the desk for a different set of papers.

On Monday morning, my son asked me to bring the dog along when I walked him to the school bus. He wanted to try something.

From the top step, he turned and gave that same little wave. The dog was busy sniffing my shoe. My son tried again the next morning.

For a week he practiced at home, stepping into another room, then waving from the doorway. Pretty soon the dog would look for his face as soon as he saw the hand.

On Friday, we walked to the bus again. My son climbed aboard and turned around.

One small wave from the top step. Beside me, the old dog lifted his gray muzzle, and his tail brushed back and forth across my shoe.

text:
Three years ago, my coworker Ogawa lost his son in Minnesota.

For eleven hours.

Ogawa had been transferred to our Minneapolis office for two years. One weekend in October, he took his wife and their five-year-old, Riku, to a little lake town two hours north. A rented cabin. Red leaves. Loons on the water. The kind of place where the gas station sells bait and pie.

At dusk, an old black Lab wandered past the cabin. Gray muzzle. Slow, friendly, tail going like a windshield wiper. Riku had always wanted a dog.

His mother looked down at her phone for maybe a minute.

When she looked up, the boy and the dog were gone. Into the trees.

By full dark, it was 34 degrees. By midnight, it would be below freezing. Riku was wearing a hoodie and one sneaker. They found the other one later.

Ogawa's wife speaks almost no English. She stood in the road screaming his name into the woods until her voice broke. Ogawa called 911 and could barely remember how to make his English work.

In Japan, when something terrible happens, we call the police, and we wait. We don't want to trouble anyone. We wait for the professionals.

In Minnesota, the professionals turned out to be anyone who owned a flashlight.

The sheriff's deputy arrived in nine minutes. Within the hour, there were pickup trucks parked along both sides of the road for half a mile. Hazard lights blinking in the dark like a runway.

Nobody had called them. Somebody posted on a town Facebook page. Somebody else told the guy at the bait shop. The bait shop guy called his brother. That was enough.

The high school football team came straight from practice, still in their jerseys.

A farmer drove his tractor out to the edge of the woods and pointed his headlights into the trees, and sat there all night, so the searchers would have something to walk back toward.

The bar on Main Street turned its sign off and its coffee maker on. The owner told Ogawa later he hadn't been inside the church across the street in thirty years. That night, he walked over and made coffee in the basement until morning.

The Lutheran ladies arrived with hotdish. Of course they did. And bars. Lemon bars. Seven-layer bars. Bars Ogawa had no word for. By midnight, there was a long folding table in the church basement covered in food, and a hand-lettered sign that just said "EAT."

One man knocked into Ogawa in the dark while running toward the woods and said "Oh, sorry, sorry, you bet" without stopping. Ogawa says it is the most Minnesotan thing he has ever seen. A man apologizing to you while he goes into the freezing woods to save your son.

Around ten o'clock, the deputies organized a grid search.

Three hundred people. Shoulder to shoulder. One arm's length apart. Flashlights pointed at the ground. A single human chain stretched across the dark fields, walking slowly into the trees together, calling a name most of them had never heard before.

"Ree-koo!"

"Rikku!"

"Rico!"

"Riku, buddy!"

Every possible way. Riku says now that he heard his name in forty different accents that night, and that's how he knew the whole world was looking for him.

In the church, Ogawa's wife sat on a metal folding chair and could not stop shaking.

An old woman sat down next to her. Eighty, maybe. A cardigan. A plastic rain bonnet. She didn't speak Japanese. Ogawa's wife didn't speak English.

So the old woman just took her hand.

And held it. All night. Without letting go. Not once. Even when her own arm went numb. Even when someone offered to take over.

At some point after two in the morning, the old woman bowed her head and began to pray. In English. Quietly.

And Ogawa's wife, without deciding to, began to pray too. In Japanese.

Two women. Two languages. One folding table. Two prayers going up into the same dark sky over Minnesota, for the same little boy.

Neither of them understood a word the other was saying.

They both understood everything.

By four in the morning, it was 27 degrees.

Some of the searchers had been out for eight hours. Nobody went home. The football players were shivering in their jerseys. Somebody's grandmother drove around the field roads with a trunk full of blankets and hand warmers, rolling down her window at every searcher: "Take one, hon. Take two."

Ogawa walked with the line. He couldn't feel his feet. He stopped calling his son's name because he couldn't make his voice work anymore.

So the men walking beside him called it for him.

At 5:12 a.m., on the far side of a frozen creek, a 79-year-old farmer named Arvid found them.

The old black Lab was his. Her name is Bear. She's twelve. She'd gotten out of the yard that evening, the way she sometimes did, and Arvid had been out all night looking for two lost things.

He found them in a hollow, under a fallen pine.

Riku was asleep.

And Bear was curled around him. All the way around. Her whole body wrapped around that little boy like a coat. Her head across his chest. Keeping the cold off him. All night long.

When Arvid's flashlight hit them, Bear lifted her head. She didn't bark. She didn't get up. She looked at him, thumped her tail twice in the frozen leaves, and stayed exactly where she was.

Like she was saying: Not yet. He's still cold.

Arvid took off his coat and wrapped the boy in it. He picked him up. Riku woke up long enough to say, in Japanese, "The doggy kept me warm."

Arvid didn't understand. He said, "I know, son. I know. She's a good girl."

He carried Riku up the hill out of the woods, in his shirtsleeves, in 27 degrees. Bear limped beside him the whole way.

At the top of the hill, three hundred flashlights saw him coming.

Someone at the end of the line shouted, "HE'S GOT HIM!"

And that shout ran down the line. Person to person. Field to field. Across three hundred people in the dark, like fire catching. "He's got him." "He's got him." "They got him."

In the church, somebody pulled the rope, and the bell started ringing. At 5:20 in the morning. Over the whole sleeping town.

Ogawa's wife heard the bell. She didn't need anyone to translate it.

She ran out of the church in her socks. Across the road. Across a frozen field. The old woman in the rain bonnet running behind her as fast as an 80-year-old can run, holding her shoes.

Ogawa says that's the moment he will see when he dies. His wife running across a white field in the first gray light, and three hundred strangers parting to let her through.

She fell to her knees in the frost and took her son from Arvid's arms.

The field went quiet.

And then someone started clapping. And then everyone. Three hundred people standing in a frozen field at dawn, clapping, crying, hugging people they didn't know. The football players were crying. The deputy was crying. Arvid was standing there in his shirtsleeves, crying, scratching his dog's ears and saying "good girl, good girl, good girl."

Then the strangest thing happened.

Everybody went home.

By seven, they were gone. The trucks pulled away one by one, hazard lights off. Some of them had work. Some of them had kids to get to school. The football players had a game Friday.

Ogawa wanted to thank them. Every single one. In Japan, a debt like this is carried for the rest of your life. You find each person. You bow. You bring gifts. You never forget.

He knew three names. The deputy. The bar owner. Arvid.

The rest of them were just gone. A church basement full of empty coffee cups. A folding table of half-eaten bars. A handwritten sign that said "EAT."

Ogawa and his family moved back to Japan the next spring.

Last summer, he went back to that little lake town. Alone. To finally pay the debt.

He brought a suitcase full of gifts from Japan. He went to the church. The bar. The bait shop.

Nobody would let him.

The bar owner hugged him and wouldn't take anything. The pastor said, "We just did what anyone would do." Arvid, now 82, took him out to the porch to see Bear. Fifteen now. Gray all over. She thumped her tail twice when she saw him, exactly like that night.

On his last morning, Ogawa sat in the diner on Main Street. The waitress, a woman around sixty, brought him coffee. When she found out who he was, she put the pot down.

"Oh my gosh. That was your boy? I made sandwiches that night. Till four in the morning."

Ogawa stood up. He bowed deeply. He tried to tell her how he had carried this for three years. How he had come all this way to repay it. How in Japan, you cannot simply accept a gift that large.

She waited until he finished.

Then she put her hand on his arm.

"Hon. You don't owe us anything.

Somebody's kid was lost.

That's all."

text:
Minnesota’s firearms deer season opens Nov. 7, 2026. Deer aged one year or older in designated southwest Minnesota permit areas require chronic wasting disease testing Nov. 7–8, with registration required before sampling.

More than 400,000 hunters are expected for the opener. That figure is an estimate, not a count of hunters who have already participated.

Every harvested deer must be registered within 48 hours of harvest. Registration and disease sampling are separate requirements: hunters bringing a deer for sampling sooner must register it first, rather than wait until the end of the registration window. The registration rule does not establish a separate 48-hour sampling deadline.

The mandatory testing requirement depends on the deer permit area and the animal’s age. It does not apply to every deer harvested anywhere in Minnesota during opening weekend, and the Nov. 7–8 sampling window is not a season-long requirement.

Testing is available statewide throughout the deer seasons, including in places where chronic wasting disease has not been detected. A mail-in program offers free kits and testing, with results available online. Kit supplies are limited.

Chronic wasting disease has not been shown to infect people. Scientists continue to study possible human health risks from contact with infected animals or eating their meat.

The mandatory sampling window begins with the Nov. 7 opener. Participation totals, sampling totals and test findings are not yet established.

text:
When 20,000 people booed her off the stage, one man whispered in her ear: "Don't let the bastards get you down."
October 16, 1992. Madison Square Garden.
Sinéad O'Connor was 25 years old and already one of the most recognizable voices in music. Her haunting cover of "Nothing Compares 2 U" had made her a global superstar. But on this night, she wasn't walking into an arena of fans.
She was walking into an ambush.
Two weeks earlier, Sinéad had done something unthinkable on live television. On Saturday Night Live, she had performed an a cappella version of Bob Marley's "War," changing the lyrics to protest child abuse. Then, staring directly into the camera, she held up a photograph of Pope John Paul II, tore it into pieces, and said two words: "Fight the real enemy."
The backlash was instantaneous and brutal.
Death threats poured in. Radio stations banned her music. The Catholic Church condemned her. Even other artists distanced themselves. Frank Sinatra said he wanted to "kick her in the ass." Joe Pesci, hosting SNL the following week, said if he'd been there, he would have "gave her such a smack."
But Sinéad didn't apologize. She didn't back down. She tried to explain—she was protesting the systemic child abuse within the Catholic Church, abuse that was being covered up at the highest levels. But in 1992, nobody wanted to hear it. The idea that the Catholic Church was protecting pedophile priests was considered conspiracy theory, anti-Catholic bigotry, the ramblings of a troubled young woman.
So when she arrived at Madison Square Garden for Bob Dylan's 30th Anniversary Concert, she knew what was coming.
The concert was a star-studded event—Neil Young, Eddie Vedder, Eric Clapton, George Harrison. Legends everywhere. And then there was Sinéad, the woman America wanted to destroy.
Kris Kristofferson was chosen to introduce her. He was a legend himself—a Rhodes Scholar, an Army Ranger captain turned songwriter, the man who wrote "Me and Bobby McGee" and "Sunday Mornin' Comin' Down." He had lived enough life to recognize courage when he saw it.
As Sinéad waited backstage, the tension was suffocating. She could hear the crowd—20,000 people who had already decided she was the villain.
Kris walked out to introduce her. He kept it simple, dignified. He said her name.
The booing started immediately.
It wasn't a scattered response. It was a WALL of sound—a unified, hateful roar that seemed to shake the rafters of Madison Square Garden. Boos, jeers, catcalls. People were standing, shouting, making obscene gestures. This wasn't a rejection of a performance. This was a mob calling for blood.
Sinéad walked out onto that stage—a tiny woman with a shaved head, wearing baggy clothes that seemed to swallow her frame—and the noise intensified. The contempt was physical, like a wave trying to push her back into the wings.
She was supposed to sing "I Believe in You," a Dylan song about faith in the face of rejection. But she couldn't. The hatred was too loud, too overwhelming. She stood there, frozen, as the booing continued.
Then she did something extraordinary.
Instead of singing the planned song, she started to scream-sing Bob Marley's "War"—the same song she'd performed on SNL, the same words that had caused the controversy: "Until the philosophy which holds one race superior and another inferior is finally and permanently discredited and abandoned... Until the color of a man's skin is of no more significance than the color of his eyes... Until that day, the dream of lasting peace will remain but a fleeting illusion."
She wasn't singing anymore. She was fighting back. Her voice was raw, defiant, angry. She was saying: If you're going to destroy me, I'm going down standing.
The booing got louder. People were throwing things. The hostility was so intense that security guards moved closer to the stage.
Sinéad couldn't finish. The wall of hate was impenetrable. She stopped mid-verse and walked off.
Kris Kristofferson met her in the wings.
She was shaking—adrenaline, rage, humiliation all colliding at once. Tears were streaming down her face. She looked like she might collapse.
Kris put his arms around her, pulled her close, and whispered directly into her ear: "Don't let the bastards get you down."
In that moment—surrounded by people who wanted to erase her, in an industry that was turning its back on her, in a culture that had decided she deserved to be punished—one person saw her clearly. Not as a publicity stunt. Not as a troubled celebrity. But as a young woman telling the truth at enormous personal cost.
Kris later wrote a song for her. He called it "Sister Sinead." The lyrics captured something essential about what he'd witnessed that night—a person too brave to be broken, too honest to be tamed, too true to flicker out.
The song acknowledged the obvious question everyone was asking: Was she crazy? Maybe. But so were all the people throughout history who saw things others couldn't see, who spoke truths others weren't ready to hear. Picasso was called crazy. The saints were called crazy. Every prophet, every truth-teller, every person who refused to stay silent when silence was easier—they were all called crazy first.
And then, years later, the world caught up.
In 2002—ten years after Sinéad tore up that photo—the Boston Globe published an investigation that changed everything. They revealed what Sinéad had been trying to say: the Catholic Church had been systematically covering up child sexual abuse for decades. Priests were molesting children, and bishops were protecting the priests. It wasn't a conspiracy theory. It was documented fact.
The revelations spread worldwide. Ireland, where Sinéad was from, was particularly devastated by the findings. Thousands of victims came forward. The cover-ups were extensive, institutional, and exactly what Sinéad had been trying to expose.
She had been right all along.
But by then, her career was already destroyed. The public eventually admitted she'd been telling the truth, but they never really apologized. She never got her moment of vindication on that same Madison Square Garden stage. The industry that blacklisted her never came back with an offer to make things right.
Sinéad O'Connor spent the rest of her life dealing with mental health struggles, fighting to be heard, trying to make music in an industry that had branded her as "difficult" and "unstable." She converted to Islam in 2018, taking the name Shuhada' Sadaqat. She continued to speak truth, continued to refuse to be what others wanted her to be.
In July 2023, Sinéad O'Connor died at age 56. The tributes poured in—many from the same people and institutions that had destroyed her decades earlier. They called her a "prophet." They praised her "courage." They acknowledged she had been right about the Church abuse.
But she never heard those tributes. She died knowing that telling the truth had cost her everything.
Kris Kristofferson—the man who whispered those words in her ear—understood something that night in 1992 that most people didn't.
He understood that history is full of people who were punished for being right too early. He understood that courage looks a lot like craziness when you're the only one standing. He understood that the people who change the world are almost always destroyed first and celebrated later.
In that moment backstage, he couldn't give her back her career. He couldn't make the booing stop. He couldn't protect her from what was coming—the years of exile, the struggle, the pain.
But he could do one thing: He could see her. Really see her. Not as the villain the mob had decided she was, but as his sister in the ancient tradition of truth-tellers who refuse to be silenced.
"Don't let the bastards get you down."
Five words that said: I know what you did was brave. I know why you did it. I know they'll make you pay for it. But don't you dare let them convince you that you were wrong.
Twenty years after that night, Sinéad finally spoke publicly about what Kris had done for her. She said those words—whispered in a moment when the whole world was screaming—had kept her alive. When she wanted to give up, when she thought maybe they were right and she was just crazy, she remembered: Kris Kristofferson believed her.
Sometimes that's all it takes. One person who refuses to join the mob. One person who stands with you when standing with you costs them something. One person who whispers the truth when everyone else is screaming lies.
Sinéad O'Connor was 25 years old when she walked onto that stage. She was just a young woman trying to protect children from the institution that had failed to protect them. She paid for that courage with her career, her reputation, and ultimately, many would argue, her life.
But she never stopped telling the truth.
And decades later, when the world finally admitted she was right, it was too late for her to hear it.
There's a lesson in this that we keep refusing to learn: The people we call crazy today might be the prophets we celebrate tomorrow. The voices we silence might be the ones we most needed to hear. The women we tear down for being "too much"—too angry, too loud, too honest—might be the only ones brave enough to say what everyone else is too afraid to say.
Sinéad O'Connor tore up a photograph to protect children. The world tore her apart for it.
And when she needed someone to stand with her, one man did.
Don't let the bastards get you down.
Those five words mattered then. They matter now. They'll matter forever.
[Harshasai OMG]

text:
Sun Tzu 7.33-35

33. It is a military axiom not to advance uphill against the enemy, nor to oppose him when he comes downhill.

34. Do not pursue an enemy who simulates flight; do not attack soldiers whose temper is keen.

35. Do not swallow bait offered by the enemy. Do not interfere with an army that is returning home.

***

Know the situation your opponent is in. Know his morale and his opportunities.

Keep your options open about when to engage and disengage. Capitalize when conditions are best.

In the context of polemics and public debate, consider which ground you are on for a given engagement. 

Do you know that you are likely to be dog piled? 

Do you have allies ready to jump to your defense? 

Who is the audience? 

Will anyone be helped by seeing what you are doing? 

What is the intention of your opponent? 

Does he plan to engaged in good faith? 

Or does he plan to draw out some statement from you in order to mock it?

How committed is your opponent to the outcome that he seeks? 

Is this the time to draw increased exposure or to let the discussion die down and be forgotten?

These questions can only be answered by attending to the details of the situation.

text:
I, for one, believe in the true concept of freedom. Some of the same people who profess a belief in the Constitution and liberty, will also support forcing someone to not sell his property. Sometimes, people own property and are flat broke otherwise, so it is not always a matter of love of money. The sale of that property could have been someone's retirement.

I for one prefer as little government involvement in anything as possible. I do not need the police for anything other than coming to clean up the mess if someone breaks into my house, God forbid. I don't need government health department checking on my restaurant, because my standard of cleanliness is much higher than theirs. Same with building code enforcement. People should not need a permit from government to building a structure on their own property.

Being we are a republic guaranteed the common law, what you refer to as "law" isn't because it does not apply to living men and women. Most Americans, including attorneys, have no idea what law in America is. 

In the long run, if I own the property, it is mine to do with as I please and if you don't like what I want to do with it, offer me enough in exchange for it to change my mind. You may not always be able to do so, like the lady who held onto her farm.

text:
Charlotte could offer Kemba Walker up to $221 million. Reports put their offer around $160 million. He left for Boston at $141 million over four years.

In 2019 he was a three-time All-Star, All-NBA, and Charlotte's all-time leading scorer.

Only the Hornets could offer the five-year supermax, worth up to $221 million. Other teams were capped at about $141 million over four years.

Walker said before free agency he would take less than the supermax to help Charlotte build a roster. His first priority was the Hornets.

The Charlotte Observer reported the Hornets' offer came in under $170 million, about $160 million over five years, over luxury-tax concerns. Owner Michael Jordan would not approve crossing the tax line for a team not built to contend.

Hornets GM Mitch Kupchak said the team offered Walker more money and more years than anybody else could.

Walker signed with Boston for four years and $141 million in a sign-and-trade. Charlotte got Terry Rozier on three years and $58 million.

On The Old Man and the Three, Walker said if Charlotte had made a max offer, he would have taken it, no question. He says he did not want to leave and still lives there.

He says if he was not getting his max, he should not be there, and that he felt he was worth more.

Knee injuries later limited him in Boston. The Celtics traded him to Oklahoma City. He agreed to a buyout and gave back about $20 million, then signed with the Knicks.

The case for Walker:
He was the face of the franchise and All-NBA. He said he would take less than $221 million. Charlotte still came in around $160 million.
He says he did not want to leave and still lives in Charlotte.
He later left another $20 million on the table in a buyout to keep playing.

The case for Charlotte:
They say they offered more total dollars and more years than any other team was allowed to offer.
A supermax would have pushed them into the luxury tax on a non-contender.
His knees failed soon after, and Boston moved him within two years.

Is it fair that Charlotte let Walker walk rather than pay closer to the max?
